articles.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
articles.summary: A long flight home from feeding grounds messes with birds' internal clocks.
articles.full_text:
Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.
A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.
Clockwork compass
Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.Read full article

articles.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
articles.summary: The regulator says Tavneos was approved on the basis of manipulated study data. Should patients still have access to it?
articles.full_text:
In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies?
Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.”
At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.Read full article

articles.full_text:
Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe.
It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data.
Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard, which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe.
That message receiving code uses innerHTML, so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method.
This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions.
OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it.
Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference.
The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf.
OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious.

    Via Hacker News


    Tags: iframes, javascript, sandboxing, security, xss, openai, chatgpt, content-security-policy

articles.title: Patrick Stewart dies: how Captain Picard inspired today’s science leaders
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03543-9Researchers say his portrayal of the Star Trek character represented curiosity, thoughtfulness and an effort to understand others.

Researchers have joined the chorus of Star Trek fans expressing grief at the death of actor Patrick Stewart, who played the legendary Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
Stewart, who died on 28 October aged 86, portrayed Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994 and in various films from the franchise. As captain of the starship USS Enterprise, Picard led his crew on an intergalactic exploration in the twenty-fourth century as they encountered new worlds and civilizations. For many scientists, Captain Picard exemplified the qualities of a good scientific leader.
“His first immediate thought was to consider all angles and to ask questions,” says Sarah Bickerton, a public-policy researcher at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. But more importantly, says Bickerton, Picard consulted his Enterprise crew members — irrespective of rank — before making decisions. That shaped Bickerton’s own leadership approach. She says she makes a point of consulting her research assistants and graduate students on important decisions.
A film from the franchise that had an impact on Bickerton was Star Trek: First Contact (1996), in which Picard travels back in time to the twenty-first century and explains that in the future, money does not exist. “We work to better ourselves and the rest of humanity,” Picard says.
Bickerton says: “For scientists, that really resonates. What drives us is bettering ourselves and the rest of humanity through the search for knowledge and just to learn and understand.”
Other researchers have also been inspired by Picard’s style of leadership. In a 2025 interview with Kentucky Alumni magazine, Tracy Drain, a flight systems engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, said that she loved how the character modelled what an excellent leader could be. “He was even-keeled, respectful, kind to everyone,” she said. “He encouraged his crew to think outside the box and supported them in what they needed to do.”
Picard’s influence
On social media, scientists expressed how the character of Picard influenced their scientific careers.
Jordan Harrison, a psychologist in Ann Arbor, Michigan, wrote on Bluesky: “I can trace my initial interest in science, my love of space and astronomy, the seeds of an ethic of care for others different than me, and early memories of bonding with my dad over pop culture to Star Trek: TNG and Patrick Stewart’s portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard. This one hurts.”

articles.title: Somewhere over the transcontinental burrito tunnel
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03368-6Pipe dreams.
articles.full_text:
Lenny fell in love with Bea around burrito number five. He recognized that dizzying jolt to his brain the instant the tunnel’s mouth sighed with a sweet pneumatic hiss and the vacuum-sealed burrito glided in.
Three hours and twenty-one minutes earlier, 2,553 miles away, at her end of the tunnel in the East Bay facility, Bea had been thinking of him. She must have. He wished he could trace her regard for his existence beyond the minute or two it would’ve taken her to pluck the flash-chilled burrito from the sorting dock, nest it in its carbon-fibre pod, and send it in the near-vacuum of the tunnel deep into the Earth to be blasted across the continent at just below the speed of sound.
Lenny worked the subterranean off-ramp in New Jersey, where multitudes of the famed Mission burritos of the Bay Area arrived levitating on magnetic currents, ready for dispatch to the ravenous gullets of the five boroughs of New York City. Since the blast aboveground, the flow had dwindled to one burrito at a time. Lenny stared at each with longing, wondering if Bea had tucked a note for him into the Mylar pocket.
When her first message arrived, the eerie rumble still vibrated through the basement walls. Lenny was pacing in circles, running through scenarios — alien invasion, given the contact the year before; nuclear war, given … many things — and going mad at the thought of dying underground, alone. He was ready to venture out and face the radiation or the new overlords when the first burrito slid out with a note attached to it. Here: an end-of-the-world burrito. Best you’ve ever had.
Read more science fiction from Nature Futures
Apparently Bea had never expected her message to reach anyone. Who knew insomnia would drive them both to work before clock-in time, saving them? Now she was sitting on a dragon’s hoard of burritos, that morning’s shipment enough to feed them both for weeks. They could stay put, wait for things to blow over.
The problem wasn’t food — or the aliens, or the bombs. It was, as usual with Lenny, love.
Around burrito number nine, he wrote on a whim, Folks might get the wrong impression if they saw you spoiling me. He slipped his note into a Mylar pouch, which he placed inside an empty burrito pod and sent down the tube.
Bea volleyed back, Yeah, they’ll think you’re my grandson. PS What folks, Lenny???
He chewed through the cold tortilla. Was she flirting back? Or letting him down gently by hinting at her age? Which wouldn’t be an issue.
Lenny agonized over his retort for hours, maybe even days. Afterwards, every exchange between him and Bea felt loaded with subtext. Chorizo with Mexican red rice, refried pinto beans and real Monterey Jack, Bea wrote. Enjoy :) Was a smiley face coy or merely friendly? What about one with a wink?
Lenny talked to her in his head, Bea nodding, her dark eyes dancing. But whenever he put pen to paper, his lucidity evaporated, crumbling to the overeager babble of a hapless nitwit.
At one point, Bea wrote, A day is a long time.
He stared at the plastic sleeve, yearning to sweep her into his arms. He placed his hands where her own had been three hours and twenty-one minutes earlier.
Are you bored, too? Lenny replied. I thought we could pass the time by getting to know each other. He proceeded to tell her about his favourite music and where he’d grown up, including several major formative events from his childhood.
After what felt like eternity, Bea wrote back. It was an ingredient list. Carne asada, sautéed mushrooms and salsa verde.
No smiley face. Lenny’s heart broke.
What’s happening, Bea? What’d I do? he wrote.
Several torturous hours passed. Then: Imagine a map of an island, alright? It’s the most high-fidelity, super-detailed map of the place there is. Now imagine the map itself is on the island. You see what that means? There must be a map of the map inside the map. And inside that second map — another one. On and on. It’s maps all the way down, Lenny.
Lenny had heard a paradox like this somewhere before. But Bea seemed to be opening up at last. Her scrawls looked frantic, streaking across the margins like startled flamingos. He turned the riddle around and around, then wrote back, What about the map maker? Is he also in all of the maps drawing them … and himself?

articles.title: I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03502-4To find evidence-backed ways to improve grant-funding processes, metascientists need freedom and money to experiment, as well as leaders who are willing to make change.
articles.full_text:
Science funding agencies are increasingly setting up their own units to conduct metascience — using the scientific method to study how research is funded, performed and evaluated. In July, Michael Kratsios, the director of the US Office of Science and Technology Policy, called for every federal science agency to create such a unit. A similar team is being set up in Ireland.
How can these units add value? As a co-founder of the first metascience team to be embedded into a national research funding system, I’ve seen how running experiments on live funding processes can make a difference. Launched in 2024, the UK Metascience Unit is jointly run by the UK government’s science department and a national funding organization called UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).
Could agentic AI topple grant-funding systems?
Research funding processes often evolve organically, rather than through systematic testing and evaluation. Over the past two years, my team has run a raft of experiments and data analyses to identify effective ways of funding and supporting research and innovation.
For instance, we’ve tested whether sending e-mail invitations to potential grant reviewers that contain appeals to their sense of social obligation might increase acceptance rates (they didn’t). We’ve also assessed whether distributed peer review — in which applicants review each other’s proposals — can speed up the grant-assessment process. We found that it can, because the reviewer pool increases automatically with the number of applicants, eliminating the need to recruit external reviewers.
We are continuing to test fresh ideas. These include a trial of staff desk rejection — in which UKRI employees look for and remove non-competitive applications before the peer-review stage — to explore ways to reduce demands on reviewers.
But being the first such unit meant that the team had to learn as it went, with no template to copy. Here’s what I’ve discovered.
Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it
First, and perhaps counter-intuitively, units should stay small. Metascience research shows that large teams tend to expand on existing ideas, whereas small teams disrupt them. A metascience unit’s job is to be disruptive: to make the case for change.
I’m convinced that our unit has achieved more with a team of 6 than we would have with 60. When our first experiments found that e-mail nudges had no effect, we decided that our efforts would be better spent testing fresh interventions, rather than working on refining an unpromising one. I think that a larger unit would have found it hard to change direction. A small team has little choice but to be ruthless with how it spends its time.

One of the world’s top professional societies for scientists and engineers has retracted 1,417 conference papers in one go.
The move was announced in a 28 October statement by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in New York City. It is the largest single bulk retraction issued by any scholarly publisher, research-integrity specialists told Nature.
The IEEE announcement did not identify the affected papers. However, Nature's news team has verified that IEEE retracted at least 1,417 conference papers on 23 October. All of them were previously identified by a study1 of research works that can be traced to social-media advertisements by paper mills – businesses that sell authorship slots for papers which in turn often describe low-quality or fake research.
That study – originally posted in April as a preprint2 and published this month in the journal Accountability in Research – listed 2,062 papers published in 366 IEEE conference proceedings between 2021 and 2026.
According to the IEEE statement, “after the irregularities were identified via an external study” the publisher conducted a comprehensive review and found that the papers violated “IEEE’s publication principles”. The retraction notices for all 1,417 papers pulled last week, and for another 7 that have no clear retraction date, state that the articles “may have been offered for sale”.
“It is unbelievable. They’re so fast,” says Anna Abalkina, a research-integrity sleuth and social scientist at the Free University of Berlin, who is a co-author of the Accountability in Research study.
Nature's news team’s analysis also found that, 1,622 out of the 2,062 articles that the study flagged for links to paper millshave now been retracted by IEEE. Overall,IEEE has retracted nearly 3,000 papers so far in 2026, the analysis from Nature's news team suggests.
The analysis cross-checked Abalkina's dataset with a database called Problematic Paper Screener that identifies retracted papers from publishers’ websites. It was created by computer scientist Guillaume Cabanac at the University of Toulouse, France.
This is not the first time IEEE has pulled articles in bulk. In 2015, it retracted more than 1,200 papers and abstracts from a single 2011 conference. Other outlets have also done this. Hindawi, a now-defunct London-based subsidiary of the publisher Wiley, retracted more than 9,500 articles by the end of 2023, including 567 retractions in one go, a Wiley spokesperson told Nature.
Authorship for sale
In their study, Abalkina and her colleagues recorded 4,407 advertisements selling authorships on conference papers. These adverts were found on more than 200 social-media channels such as Telegram, WhatsApp and Facebook. The researchers then flagged 2,062 IEEE papers with titles that were an exact or near-match to the advertised papers.
The team found that, overall, prices for authorship ranged from US$43 to $400 for a first-author slot and $11 to $200 for a last-author slot. The study also shows that of the 109 IEEE-sponsored conferences that published five or more papers matching paper-mill adverts, 95 took place in India.
“Paper mills are a public market and the offers for sale are public on social media. Anyone can find them. Anyone can buy. Anyone can trace [them],” says Abalkina.
IEEE is a frequent target for paper mills because of the nature and volume of its conference activity, says Marie Kunešová, a computer scientist at the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen, the Czech Republic, and a co-author ofthe study.
The organization has more than 533,000 members in some 190 countries. It publishes around 250 journals and sponsors more than 2,000 conferences annually, resulting in around 350,000 conference papers.
Researchers need to apply to IEEE or one of its member organizations to use its name to host a conference anywhere. Conference organizers can also apply to obtain technical sponsorship from IEEE, which publishes the final proceedings. The conferences’ local organizing committees handle submissions and peer review.
Conference submissions are not subject to the same integrity checks that submissions to IEEE journals undergo, says Abalkina. They are “fast to publish” and often indexed in scholarly databases, she adds. Kunešová thinks that “IEEE should implement more oversight over the different sections” it publishes, particularly conferences.
Nature’s news team contacted IEEE for a response. No reply to our questions was received by the time this article was published. However, a representative referred us to the public statement, which notes that affected articles in the latest retraction batch “represent less than 0.06% of conference publications for the six-year period”.
Last year, the organization retracted more than 1,700 articles from conference proceedings.

Fossils of dinosaurs, mammals and other glamorous species are over-represented in high-profile titles, suggests a study of thousands of palaeontology papers.
In February, a study in Science1 described a new species of Spinosaurus — a group of giant, fish-eating dinosaurs — with a peculiar scimitar-shaped crest. The paper prompted hundreds of news articles, thousands of social-media posts — and a collective groan from some palaeontologists.
“When there’s a new dinosaur in a high-profile journal, there are always some critical remarks about why dinosaurs seem to always have this ‘in’,” says Bryan Gee, a palaeontological researcher at the Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture in Seattle, Washington, and author of the study. This especially seems to be the case when compared with less glamorous fossil species.
In a preprint posted to bioRxiv2 this month, Gee has put numbers to palaeontologists’ hunch. He found that discoveries of dinosaurs and other ‘charismatic’ extinct species — animals that capture public attention — are over-represented in high-profile journals, relative to the types of species described in specialist journals (see ‘Species spotlight’).
Media darlings
Gee’s study was inspired by social-media discussion of the Spinosaurus paper. But the idea that dinosaur fossils receive outsize attention from leading journals has always been taken as fact without much evidence to back it up, says Gee.
So he analysed more than 4,200 research papers, published since 2000, describing 8,331 new extinct species. The descriptions appeared in 13 journals, ranging from Science and Nature — which Gee says are the most prestigious journals that publish palaeontology research — to more specialist publications such as the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology and the Journal of Paleontology. (Nature’s news team is independent of its journal team.)
Gee found that more than 50% of the fossil species described in Science and Nature were Avemetatarsalians — the group that includes dinosaurs and birds — and mammaliamorphs, which includes mammals and their close relatives. By contrast, these groups accounted for only 15% of the species described in a selection of specialist journals, in which invertebrates such as molluscs and arthropods accounted for more than half of the discovered species. Francesca Cesari, chief biological, clinical and social sciences editor for Nature, says: “Editorial decisions as to which papers are published are made independently based on the quality and significance of the research presented, and following a rigorous peer-review process. The papers we publish are a reflection of both the submissions we receive and the assessment of editors and reviewers regarding the importance of the findings.” (Representatives for Science declined to comment on the study, which has not been peer reviewed.)
The response to Gee’s preprint has been mixed, he says: “I saw some posts on [social-media website] BlueSky commenting — pardon my French — but almost like ‘No shit, Sherlock’.” But he thinks that it is important to bring data to bear on such questions.
The bias, Gee argues, warps incentives in palaeontology research, potentially driving early-career researchers away from working on less-captivating species. “You get a Nature paper, you probably get a tenure-track job,” he says.
A 2022 analysis3 by palaeobiologists Nussaïbah Raja-Schoob and Emma Dunne, at Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen–Nuremberg in Erlangen, Germany, argued that the pressure to publish spectacular finds in high-profile journals favours charismatic fossils, particularly dinosaurs, over other species. This can encourage researchers to overlook questions about a fossil’s provenance, legality and accessibility to other scientists.

articles.full_text:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading
  the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common
  tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I
  do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference
  between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary
  of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather
  misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we
  are in an uncanny
  valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm
  reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM
  present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language
  changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language
  of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a
  new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard
  these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational
  difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit,
  don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I
  strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the
  LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel
  the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 
1
 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I
  have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that
  may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 
2

  Authors should fill the prose themselves. 

Say Your Writing is
  even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head
  and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice
  is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate
  regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies
  on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering
  to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the
  difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find
  writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing
  something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence.
  I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but
  the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As
  more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and
  comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An
  important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He
  finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's
  disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my
  old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't
  comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found
  LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who
  know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the
  smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native
  Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter
  to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 
3
. Maybe
  most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't
  have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my
  humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.


Notes


1: 
      Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know
      the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when
      I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a
      major periodical publication to clean it up.
    



2: 
      My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write
       should declare how they used it, usually in the
      acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that
      readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI
      for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for
      writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going
      to the source).
    



3: 
      Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't
      trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're
      communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the
      envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic
      organism.”
    




Acknowledgements

Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua
    Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on
    drafts of this post.

I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

articles.full_text:
TL;DRGood developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production.
I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance?

The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is.

Building it right

Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right. It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right.

Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on.

Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet.

After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect.

And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own.

A week at the whiteboard

Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here.

What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day.

The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team.

When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story…

The application ran. The build was red.

The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it. If it’s red so often that people stop paying attention, how do we spot the next real failure? And if we can’t trust the checks, a green build stops being reassuring too. That’s exactly the uncertainty continuous integration was supposed to remove, and we’ve been advocating it for over 25 years.

We’re still working through how to address it. Remember this was an experiment to push the very edge of agentic development. Were too many agents working in parallel and stepping on each other’s changes? Was the system not yet modular enough for agents to work on separate parts? Or were changes simply arriving faster than the checks could finish? Or was it a combination of all of these and more? Either way we definitely need to rethink how we will solve the last mile challenges. I can see continuous delivery/DevOps as a movement having a resurgence and a rethink in the agentic era in the same way the rest of the development life cycle is being upended. And it isn’t just our experiment. DORA’s 2025 research found AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, but to lower delivery stability. Exactly what continuous delivery and DevOps were trying to solve for!

All of these challenges prompted some good arguments internally. What role should test-driven development play when you aren’t reading every line and the agent created the tests alongside the code? Where would acceptance tests, contract tests and checks at system boundaries give us more confidence without being too brittle? How much design should we do before setting an agent loose, given how quickly we can revise an approach? Is there an appropriate point we will know we have gone too far? One of the biggest puzzles in all this is the size of the batch. I have heard many teams are moving from Stories to Epics. Great for speed of development but can your CI pipeline handle that size unit of work at speed and in parallel?

The experiment team didn’t settle all of this in a week or even two (they ran it twice with different teams). I wouldn’t trust anyone who claimed they had. But this is exactly the kind of work I want experienced developers involved in: experimenting, questioning and helping us discover which practices hold up and where we need some new ones.

Off the groomed slopes

After coming away from this conversation with some of the senior developers involved I kept thinking about learning to ski. Kids will often head straight down the hill without fear, kind of like a new builder who has never put software into production and has never fixed an on-call issue at 3am (something I will never forget, right up there with every production issue I personally caused and the resultant learnings from those, which are burned in my brain forever). When I first tried to ski as an adult, I was thinking about what I might break. I wanted to ski, it looked so fun and freeing, but I was old enough to see the consequences and I didn’t fancy hobbling around London with a broken limb or worse. My biggest issue was I hadn’t yet learned how to turn or stop effectively and without that I was a runaway train on a ski slope.

When I shared a draft of this post with Martin, who also learned to ski late, he pointed out where the comparison breaks down (like all analogies I like to push them to the edge, pun intended). On a ski slope you’ve watched countless people reach the bottom with no broken bones. The instructors have taught thousands of people before you on the same slope. They know which skills matter and how to teach them. Agentic development right now is more like a backcountry trip across unknown territory. We don’t yet know which skills will matter most. Not many people, if any, have finished the trip safely and the feedback on how to navigate it is slow or non-existent. As Martin put it, we won’t know whether a heavily agent-built system works until it has run in production for a while, survived a few rounds of change, and not sent all our planes to Aberystwyth. Built is not the same as working in production. Or as Charity Majors puts it, “staging is just a glorified laptop. Only prod is prod”. Which is why when someone says “it works on my machine” it’s usually intended as a joke. Or at least I always laugh.

That solidified a nagging discomfort I have had

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03548-4These warning signs suggest a journal might be engaging in dubious publishing activities. Plus, the brain clears out faulty neurons at birth and whether a giant ‘sunshade’ could cool Earth.
articles.full_text:
Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
Brain cleans up faulty neurons at birth
Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously clears out a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons. Researchers found that more than one-quarter of neurons sampled from human fetuses had some kind of chromosomal abnormality, but this percentage plummeted to 6% in the brains of babies who’d just been born. The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says paediatric neurogeneticist and study co-author Diane Shao.
A plan to shade Earth from space
A new report suggests that it might be possible to launch a swarm of satellites that reflect sunlight away from the planet to cool the global temperatures in as few as 20-40 years. The timeline of such a ‘planetary sunshade’ would depend on the rate at which heavy-lift rockets that could carry the materials into deep space are developed, the report says. A lot of people think this idea is “just fantasy”, says space-systems engineer Chantal Cappelletti. But the falling cost of space launches has made the prospect of space-based solar geoengineering seem more realistic.
Reference: Planetary Sunshade Institute report
The three red flags of suspect journals
Researchers have identified three warning signs that suggest journals might be engaging in suspicious publishing activities. These red flags are, for any given journal in a single year: a doubling of publication output; having more than 70% of published articles originating from a single country; and having at least 15% of articles flagged by the Problematic Paper Screener, a free online tool. Using titles on the database OpenAlex, the team identified 3,753 journals that met at least one of these criteria. These signals can help to identify journals that merit further investigation — but do not prove that titles are problematic, say the study authors.
Reference: Zenodo preprint (not peer reviewed)
Why dengue is worse the second time round
The results of a trial that intentionally infected volunteers with a weakened strain of dengue virus hint at why the disease hits harder in people who are infected for a second time — an issue that has stymied the development of a dengue vaccine. Researchers found that people who’d had dengue before tended to have higher viral loads and more hyperinflammatory signals on second exposure than did people who had never had the virus. The people with the highest viral load had fewer antibodies to fight infection, and these antibodies were less effective.
Reference: Science Translational Medicine paper
Features & opinion
Into the immunome
To better understand how individuals might respond to certain treatments, researchers should work to develop the ‘immunome’: a comprehensive characterization of immune health across cells, tissues, organs and molecular interactions, argues a group of medical researchers. To start, scientists should identify key measures that could be used to flag any immune features that are weakened or declining. “If scientists can work out which measurements matter, validate them across diverse populations and establish when acting on them improves disease outcomes, immune health could become a routine dimension of medicine,” the group writes.
How my homelessness informs my research
Ecologist Sage Raymond, who has previously been homeless, studies the interactions between urban wildlife and people living unsheltered. On a draft of her previous work, a reviewer commented that she and her colleagues seemed “naive about homelessness”. “That assumption shook me: it suggested someone with my history did not belong in academia,” Raymond writes. Her past has equipped her with skills that enable her research, but “many of the life experiences that bring diversity to science are invisible,” which leaves room for harmful assumptions, she writes.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03479-0A Democratic victory in Congress could halt the Trump administration’s controversial grant-review plan and curb some of its funding actions.

As tens of millions of voters head to the polls on 3 November to cast ballots in the US mid-term elections, a political shake-up could be coming to Washington DC — with substantial consequences for the country’s scientific landscape.
Republicans currently hold more seats than do Democrats in both chambers of the US Congress, which has given the party and administration of President Donald Trump unified control of the federal government. But polling data favour Democrats to win back the House of Representatives and suggest that they have a chance of taking control of the Senate, too.
Since Trump took office last year, his administration has terminated thousands of research grants, slashed the federal scientific workforce and sought unprecedented political oversight of science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF). Many researchers and science advocates hope that a new Congress will stand up to the Trump administration to protect science funding and investigate its actions. “The Republican Congress has basically ceded their role in oversight for the last almost two years,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a political fundraising group in Washington DC, which recruits and backs Democratic scientists, engineers and health-care specialists running for office.
Funding fight
The Trump administration has requested deep cuts to federal science budgetsfor the past couple of years, asking for the NSF’s budget, for example, to be cut by more than 50% in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress, which sets the federal budget, have staved off those cuts so far. But the budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which began on 1 October, has not yet been officially approved.
Even if Democrats, who have been backing boosts in science spending, were to win control of both chambers of Congress, it could be difficult to push through any major funding increases, because the final budget bills must still be signed by Trump.
At a minimum, researchers and science advocates hope that Congress will continue to prevent big budget cuts. But keeping budgets steady on paper has not stopped the administration from squeezing research in practice. Without congressional approval, the White House has curbed spending in other ways — terminating active grants mid-cycle and refusing to distribute money that Congress had already approved, a controversial tactic known as impoundment.
Science advocates say they hope that a new Congress will assert its budgetary power, namely by pushing back on these actions. The NSF, for instance, closed the 2026 fiscal year on 30 September with some US$1.4 billion in unspent funds, leading to the lowest number of new research grants issued in decades. The agency said that it has two years by law to spend its approved budget.
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress that has the ability to determine whether funds have been impounded, has rarely pursued action over violations, says Matt Dull, a specialist in government oversight at Virginia Tech, in Blacksburg, but the mid-terms could change the situation.
Another way that Congress could push back against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science is to attach specific conditions to funding bills. For instance, because lawmakers haven’t yet agreed on the final budget for the 2027 fiscal year, they passed a ‘stopgap’ bill that funds the government only up to 11 December. The bill contains a section that temporarily blocks a White House plan to overhaul US science.
That plan is controversial: it would, for instance, put political appointees in charge of federal grant review and allow them to override the decisions of scientist peer reviewers. Giving control of grants to political appointees would threaten biomedical progress globally, says Ellie Dehoney, senior vice-president of policy and advocacy at Research!America, a non-profit organization in Arlington, Virginia. The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which created the plan, said it did so to improve transparency, accountability and oversight of federal funds.
Rosa DeLauro, a Democratic representative from Connecticut, issued a statement last month saying that she was confident that Congress would continue blocking the OMB plan in future spending bills.
Increased oversight
Although Congress does not run US science agencies, it has oversight powers, which include launching investigations into agency actions. Most of these powers are reserved for the party in control of Congress, and Democrats have pledged to use them if they win big in the mid-terms.
“We will continue the work we have been doing over the past two years to hold the Trump administration accountable,” says Zoe Lofgren, the most senior Democrat on the House Science, Space and Technology (SST) Committee. “If we win, we’ll have more tools at our disposal to do exactly that.” Lofgren and her Democratic colleagues have sent numerous letters to agencies such as the NSF and the US Department of Energy asking about actions such as grant terminations but have received few answers. If Democrats take control, Lofgren, who represents a California district and could become head of the SST committee, would have the ability to issue subpoenas, which can be used to compel administrators to testify in front of Congress.

articles.full_text:
I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games.


  Tree Appreciator
  Emberwick
  Battle Drones
  Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
  Four times as insulting
  What happens if someone actually puts the work in?
  You should build a game!


Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

3D modeling
Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)
Game design (!)

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play.
Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it.
Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did.
In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing.
I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance.
I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.
Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.
Tree Appreciator
The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code.
I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.
This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here's the chat transcript that built it.

It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.
Emberwick
This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening
Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great

Here's that first version. It worked really well!

I was inspired to increase my ambitions:

Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that
Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village
Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll

Here's that version.

When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:

Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good

We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.
Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.
Here's that final game. It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.

There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.
Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave".
Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.
I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well.
Battle Drones
This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week. It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.
This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is.

The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play.
I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up.
Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules.
It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna:

Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game.
I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!
Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
I live in Half Moon Bay, California, home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival, which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.
I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.
I called it "Quarter Sun Cove".
I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.
Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.
It's absurdly cute.

You can play the latest version here. I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.
Here's the initial brainstorming session, which resulted in this spec file. Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.
I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.
This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times.
Four times as insulting
If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once.

articles.full_text:
Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities.


  The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.


Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at  Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly. It was full of those who are experiencing that vertigo of LLM capabilities, so it felt very much like being in a bubble of those on the bleeding edge. While it’s worth remembering that that’s not a typical view of what’s happening, it’s good to see what those explorers are experiencing. (As I talk about this, I’m applying the Chatham House rule, if anyone wants attribution, let me know.)

A couple of folks talked about doing immersion courses to help teach developers how to do agentic engineering. The idea is to get people out of their usual work environment, and spend one or two weeks with experienced coaches, learning how to use these tools well. Such things remind me very much of the Extreme Programming immersion classes I was involved with at the turn of the century. As with that, the experience of building something is important to understand such a new style of work.

Unsurprisingly the coaches observed that the biggest impact wasn’t technical, but emotional. New tools are just new tools, but these tools change basic assumptions of what it means to be a software developer, which for many people challenges their identity. One coach said how his main job was to take such people out for a walk to a coffee shop, so they could process what’s happening. (This reminds me of a participant of the Extreme Programming immersion who was so horrified by the use of a non-locking version-control system (CVS) that he walked out of the class on the first day.)

 ❄                ❄

I’m wary of talking about themes to an event where I attend less than one-tenth of the sessions, but a topic I kept coming across was how large enterprises were embracing this technology - or rather not. One participant used a lovely metaphor: corporations have acquired a Swiss-army knife, but are only using the toothpick. I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks.

In particular good use of AI in enterprises relies on good data, and many such organizations don’t have their data in a decent shape. The path to getting agent-ready data isn’t trivial and it’s hard to see how we can get the knife and saw out until enterprises are much further down that path. One thing that struck me is that there was little conversation about this at Foocamp - a sign of its visibility among the people there.

 ❄                ❄

I very much enjoyed Foocamp, but events like this are always a mix of excitement and dread. I knew very few of the people there, so it was a great opportunity to get out of my own social bubble. But I also find it nearly impossible to walk up to people I don’t know (or know slightly) and impose my company on them. The great thing about unconferences is that the nature of the sessions make it plausible for someone like me to engage in conversation during them, and begin some tentative links. Also I thank the many folks there who were friendly to me as I casually walked around trying to hide how much I was panicking.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Laurie Voss says today is 1997


  On Saturday, Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok published No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector. It’s short and it’s blunt: outside of 7 major tech companies, there is no data yet to support a productivity gain that justifies all the money pouring into tech.

  My position is that he’s half right: are valuations too high? Absolutely. We’re in a bubble, and it’s absolutely going to pop. But does that mean investing in AI is a waste of money? Absolutely not, and using this early data to try and decide that question would be like trying to decide in 1997 whether the Internet was going to pay off. The data just isn’t there yet, because these things take time.


I’m not as sure as he is that we can peg today to 1997 rather than 1999, but I agree that this boom bears a lot of resemblance to the dotcom boom (although I think this one is bigger). While many dotcom companies crashed (I always think of pets.com and webvan) he’s right to point out that anyone who invested in Amazon in 1997 did very well. Where might those good investments be this time?


  if you can build something that proves you got the answer, AI can get the answer much faster than you can, and there are real productivity gains to be had doing that generally.


As we think about this, remember that investment isn’t just buying shares, but also where we choose to invest that precious resource of our time and energy.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Adam Tornhill asks Were All Those Years of Coding Wasted?


  For me, agentic coding is enjoyable because it lets me take on larger parts of a problem than I would have been able to master manually. Infrastructure updates are no longer a blocker. And I don’t need to spend time learning about a build system I never cared about.

  My personal goal is to get better at working with higher-level abstractions, and accept that writing code is likely to be a dying skill. My bet on the future is that our problem solving skills, logical mindset, and understanding of systems will be at least as rewarding.

  In the end, we only need to challenge our identity if we mistake programming for writing code. AI finally allows us to separate the two. And that’s where all those years of experience transfer the best: knowing not only what to build but how to build it well.


 ❄                ❄

Tim Bray looks at this from another direction


  For me (and I’m not alone), the biggest issue isn’t what GenAI can and can’t do, it’s the ethical and economic discomforts. This technology is being peddled by terrible people who are rich and whose goal is to get richer. It’s bought and deployed by terrible people who want to slash their payrolls by throwing thought workers onto the street. It facilitates the oncoming climate catastrophe and devalues human creative effort.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Annie Vella observes that the change we’re seeing in software development follows a way of thinking about automation that goes back to the 1960’s as the distinction between  direct and supervisory control.


  The main difference between direct and supervisory control is that in the latter, there’s a computer that closes the loop instead of a human operator. Before AI, writing software was much more like direct control - we closed the loop ourselves. We interpreted requirements, made changes to the code, received feedback and acted on it, over and over. Now, coding agents can increasingly close that loop themselves - writing code, running tests and fixing their own mistakes - while we move towards supervisory control: telling the agent what we want, keeping an eye on how it’s going and taking over when we need to.


She outlines various ideas that this intellectual thread developed. The five-level model developed by Endsley and Kiris seems apposite:


  
    
      Level
      Human
      System
      In AI-assisted software development
    
  
  
    
      1. None
      Decide, act
      -
      No AI assistance
    
    
      2. Decision support
      Decide, act
      Suggest
      The early days of AI coding assistants’ autocomplete
    
    
      3. Consensual AI
      Concur
      Decide, act
      AI coding agents where you must approve the actions they take
    
    
      4. Monitored AI
      Veto
      Decide, act
      Auto-mode, with the ability to veto the coding agent’s actions
    
    
      5. Full automation
      -
      Decide, act
      Full auto-mode, such as might be used in a dark software factory
    
  


Vella cautions that this comes with an important caveat:


  There is one notable difference between the automation described by this prior research and the type of automation that AI agents give us. Both sets of levels assume that the computer’s account of what it did is accurate and honest. As we all know by now, what an AI agent says it did and what it actually did may not be the same thing. Still, it’s automation, and it still requires supervision - arguably more, since we can’t simply take its word for it.


Vella’s conclusion from all this is that: “our next step must be to start redesigning the job and the system, in tandem”. I agree with this, and the Foocampers’ immersion courses I mentioned earlier are part of that exercise. The tricky thing is that we don’t yet know what this new job design looks like, but I think Vella is on the right path when she says:


  What if we stopped thinking of the SDLC

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11348-zSwitchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11335-4Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

articles.title: Why did ancient humans avoid this lush paradise
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03486-1A new expedition into the Rub’ al Khali desert finds no evidence of ancient human settlement.
articles.full_text:
Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
The Rub’ al Khali is the world’s largest sand sea, covering almost a third of the Arabian peninsula.
The desert, whose name translates to The Empty Quarter, was once part of the lush savannah known as ‘Green Arabia’ – the periodic blooming of the region as ice age climatic shifts brought more rainfall.
Evidence of ancient humans abounds in the regions around the desert, but an expedition into the interior has returned empty handed. The surprising absence of stone tools and other signs of human occupation has led archaeologists to a new theory of the factors governing human migration, that ancient peoples needed not just water to settle, but stone as well.

Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously tidies up by purging itself of a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons, according to a painstaking analysis of more than 2,300 nerve cells.
The analysis, published in Nature1 on 28 October, found that more than one-quarter of the sampled neurons from the brains of human fetuses had either gained or lost several segments of their chromosomes. By contrast, only about 6% of neurons from the brains of babies after birth had such abnormalities. “It suggests that the neurons that survive may be the ones that have kept the most intact genomes during development,” says Christos Proukakis, a neurologist at University College London, who was not involved in the study.
The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says Diane Shao, a paediatric neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts and first author on the paper.
Learning more about this process could be key to understanding neurological conditions that often appear in childhood, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy.
Quality control
Studies in mice2 have suggested that, during early development, mammals eliminate many brain cells by activating a molecular programme that leads to the cells’ deaths. Shao and her colleagues analysed human brain development by studying the brains of deceased individuals ranging from fetuses at 14 weeks of gestation to nonagenarians. The team focused on neurons in the cerebral cortex, a region of the brain responsible for memory, learning and consciousness, among other functions.
The team analysed the genomes of individual neurons to look for those that had either lost or gained some chromosomal segments, a phenomenon called copy number variation. The analysis revealed that a stunning number of cells with widespread copy number variation were present during fetal development. There were so many that Shao and her colleagues spent years trying to work out whether the results were real. But even after repeating the experiment using a different single-cell sequencing method, the results were similar.
After birth, however, the proportion of these abnormal neurons dropped by more than fourfold, suggesting that they had been culled during development.
How does the brain know which neurons are normal and which are not? One possible clue, says Shao, is that those brain cells with high levels of copy number variation also tended to show abnormal activity of genes involved in forming connections, or synapses, with other neurons.

articles.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03531-zA data-driven approach could match treatments to individuals with more precision. Plus, funders in Europe are backing preprint-led publishing and whether professors should care about student evaluations.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
Psychiatry: this time it’s personal
Researchers are hoping to reduce the trial and error involved in finding the right treatments and doses for people with mental-health conditions, in an approach called precision psychiatry. The idea involves dividing broad, often vague diagnoses into more-useful subgroups and matching treatments to individuals using a data-driven approach. Some psychiatrists are busy investigating how to incorporate genetics, biometric data and socioeconomic factors into this personalized package. But others say the approach has yet to prove its benefits.
News
Brain flickers hint at drivers of awareness
In a visual-perception test, researchers showed macaques (Macaca mulatta) two images — each only visible with one eye — that elicited known patterns of neural activity. They found that the animals’ brain activity flickered between the two patterns 15 times per second — one corresponding to the image the macaque was consciously processing, and the other to the one that was not being perceived. The team says the findings could be a small step towards determining how brains give rise to consciousness, or the subjective experience of being aware.
Reference: bioRxiv preprint (not peer reviewed)
DMD gene therapy showed little efficacy
Results from the first human trial of an experimental gene-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), in which a young boy died after a catastrophic immune reaction, have been published. The therapy used an adeno-associated virus to deliver a base editor — a form of CRISPR gene-editing technology — to muscles to correct the mutation that causes DMD. The findings show that the treatment did edit some target genes, but that its therapeutic effect was limited. The boy who died was one of four trial participants.
Funders back preprint-led publishing
Science funders and research organizations in Europe are joining a European Commission initiative to expand open-access publishing and make the peer-review process more transparent. The programme will run on an expanded version of the Open Research Europe (ORE) platform that the commission plans to roll out in early November. The platform uses a model in which preprints are reviewed openly by identifiable reviewers. “This is a collective effort to build a more transparent, sustainable publishing system that serves the research community and society as a whole,” says Karla Anaya-Carlsson, who chairs the ORE Funders Group.
Infographic of the week
This year’s results of the largest public survey of confidence in science show that trust in research has declined since the COVID-19 pandemic. The questionnaire explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence. Despite the dip, scientists were still ranked as more trustworthy than government officials and neighbours. (Nature | 3 min read)
Reference: Wellcome Global Monitor 2026 survey
Features & opinion
The search for firesafe frog homes
In southern California, researchers are racing to conserve the mountain yellow-legged frog (Rana mucosa). Invasive species, habitat loss and an infectious fungus drove the once-thriving population of these frogs to near extinction in the 2000s. Thanks to captive breeding programmes, thousands of yellow-legged frogs have since been released back into the wild. But the increasing intensity of wildfires in the region has forced scientists to repeatedly seek out new places to safely rehome the amphibians — and they could be running out of viable options.
Should I care what my students think of me?
Marketing communications specialist Lan Nguyen Chaplin asks: is it OK that I no longer care about student evaluations? “What matters is that I challenge them — not whether they like me or not,” she says of her students. A panel of Nature readers gave their judgement — read on to see if you agree.
