Several years into my career, one comment from a student evaluation of my teaching stopped me cold. “I didn’t learn a thing. The professor was stingy with help and arrogant.”
I was devastated. To run this particular course, I had spent late nights answering e-mails, working extra hours in the office and redesigning assignments to prepare students for a competitive job market. But that comment forced me to confront a painful truth: the more I pushed students out of their comfort zone, the more some disliked me.
In a culture that equates popularity with success, early-career academics often treat being liked as a key metric. I’ve learnt that chasing approval ratings can undermine teaching. So I stopped worrying about student evaluations entirely.
I care about students’ happiness, but I also want to be the kind of professor who pairs care with a push for excellence. What matters is that I challenge them — not whether they like me or not.
Am I wrong? — Lan Nguyen Chaplin, specialist in integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois.
Nature reached out to other scientists to review your behaviour. Are you insensitive to the needs of your students or are you right to focus on challenging them?
Comments from the jury
“A teaching style that doesn’t seek universal popularity is usually manageable, because you work with students only for a limited time. However, leadership roles often also come with power, and with great power comes great responsibility. It is not wrong to use that authority when necessary, as long as it is exercised with fairness and care.” —Monalisa Mallick, quantum engineer at Friedrich Schiller University, Jena, Germany.
“The prof makes a fair point. But in their situation, I’d be sure to collect evidence of learning because if the students hate their professor and also don’t learn anything, it's not a good deal for anyone.” — Russ Altman,researcher in bioengineering, genetics, medicine and biomedical data science at Stanford University, California.
“It’s inevitable that you cannot be universally liked, but good leaders and teachers should still reflect on why people might feel negatively about them. A bit of self-criticism can go a long way. Dismissing criticism, instead of learning from it, I find worrying.” — Juliana Sanchez Alponti Millar,biologist at the University of York, UK.
“I strongly agree. Academic leadership should not be measured only by popularity, but also by fairness, clarity and the ability to help people grow beyond their comfort zones.” —Jay Jesús MolinoCornejo, physicist at UDELAS, Panama City.
“Totally fair! I also started out giving far too much of myself to students. Now I have firm boundaries on how much time I will spend on e-mails and preparation. It’s helped my workload and means that I don’t make my students’ feelings my own.” — Maggie Swift, conservation scientist at theCornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Wildlife Health in Ithaca, New York.
The verdict
Feedback can be a valuable tool for self-reflection, but it’s a truth universally acknowledged — both in science and in life — that you really can’t please everyone. Most respondents seem to back Nguyen Chaplin’s conviction that she was better off putting her energy into teaching in line with her values.

articles.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03402-7Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.
articles.full_text:
More than one billion people globally live with a mental-health condition. Collectively, these disorders are now the world’s leading cause of disability. Depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy an estimated US$1 trillion every year.
The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
Conventional pharmacological approaches to improving mental health are falling short. However, two Nature News features this week report on innovations that indicate a shift is under way. One describes the personalization of psychiatric care; the other discusses developments in psychedelic medicine. Although neither effort will provide a complete solution for the mental-health crisis, both are bringing much-needed ingenuity to the field.
To ensure that these ideas translate into improvements in mental-health care, they must be pursued with rigour and in a way that ensures they have the widest possible reach. As psychedelic-development programmes move towards regulatory approval, the US Food and Drug Administration has rightly clarified what types of evidence and outcome it expects to see in trials (see go.nature.com/4bstrh2). Funders and regulators must now ensure that approaches that prove successful actually reach the people who need them. This will not be straightforward because many psychedelics and proposed personalized treatments are expensive. They are developed with small groups of people with a specific condition in mind and therefore do not benefit from economies of scale. At the same time, personalized treatments can be out of reach for people from low-income backgrounds, who are more likely than others to have a mental-health condition.
Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
Under the current psychiatric model for mental-health conditions, two people with the same diagnosis of depression can have distinct symptoms, different underlying biology and divergent responses to the same treatments. That heterogeneity is reflected in clinical outcomes. A substantial proportion of people don’t respond to the first antidepressant drug that they try, and around 30% remain symptomatic after trying several treatments (C. Njenga et al. BMJ 386, e073823; 2024).
In practice, conditions are more complex than conventional diagnostic categories suggest. One reason for this is that classifications have relied on subjective reporting of symptoms. Now, precision psychiatry approaches aim to improve diagnosis and outcomes. The idea is to personalize treatments by cataloguing symptoms in detail and as objectively as possible, and identifying measurable biological indicators, or biomarkers. The expectation is that this can help to match people with more-effective treatments, and do so faster by shortening the process.
Methods include the use of genetic and blood-based biomarkers; measures of brain activity such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalograms; and ‘digital phenotyping’, in which smartphones and other sensors record sleep and movement, for instance. But these assessments have yet to consistently yield improvements for people with mental-health conditions, as one of the features reports. Some researchers say that another approach would be to gather as much data as possible on how people respond to specific treatments and which responses correlate with mental-health improvements. Those data can then be fed into artificial-intelligence models to predict how individuals might fare. It is unclear, however, whether the benefits of such tools would outweigh their costs.
Psychedelics: concerns and opportunities
As reported in the other feature, psychedelics might tap into the brain’s capacity to reorganize its connections and circuits, potentially disrupting rigid patterns and enabling psychological changes — even for some people for whom conventional treatments haven’t worked.
The ‘bible for psychiatry’ is getting a rewrite: your guide to the next DSM
Outcomes could be optimized by personalization. But, as with precision psychiatry more broadly, this approach comes with a duty to prioritize research into treatment responses across diverse populations. The use of psychedelics introduces additional concerns. Adequately trained health-care workers are needed to bolster the drug’s efficacy and safety, especially during potentially intense, unpredictable and lengthy psychedelic experiences.
Existing treatments for mental-health conditions, including psychotherapy and antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can be extremely effective for some people. But their full therapeutic benefits can take time to emerge. The rapid relief provided by psychedelics could complement such therapies.
However, even the most sophisticated and effective treatment strategies will have limited impact if people can’t access them. That’s why funders and regulators must work out who is going to cover the cost of a brain scan (if they are found to be clinically useful) or pay for a hours-long session so people can take psychedelics safely. Someone will need to assess whether these approaches have enough benefits to offset the spiralling costs of mental-health care — and whether those benefits can be provided equitably.
US speeds up research into mind-altering drugs — including mysterious ‘ibogaine’
There are ways to reduce upfront costs as well as expand reach, for example, by using low-cost biomarkers and therapy sessions in which participants take psychedelic substances together in a supervised setting. Several studies have found that such group sessions can even enhance the therapeutic effects in some cases (A. L. Back et al. Psychedelic Med. 4, 209–221; 2026). Psychedelics with briefer hallucinogenic effects, currently under development, might be an alternative, too.
However, progress on diagnoses and treatments should be paired with innovation on another front: preventing people from developing a mental-health disorder in the first place. No medical breakthroughs can substitute for a society that supports good mental health — and more could be done to reduce the factors that contribute to mental illness, such as economic insecurity, sleep disruption, environmental pollution and social isolation.
The field’s willingness to consider how to reinvent psychiatry is welcome. Proponents of the ideas must now ensure that all who can benefit have access to these therapies and that the highest standards of quality and rigour are adhered to.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03261-2A cellular fuel called lactate is channelled directly into energy-generating organelles in heart muscle, defying the prevailing view about lactate transport.

Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
Lactate is abundant in human blood and is crucial for systemic metabolism. Although it has been studied for centuries, there is still controversy about how this molecule is handled by cells. One long-standing debate is about the mechanism by which lactate-derived carbons make their way into mitochondria to fuel the production of energy-carrying ATP molecules. Writing in Nature, Cluntun et al.1 provide solid support for a conclusion that defies current dogma: in the heart, lactate can enter mitochondria directly through a specific transporter protein and this process is essential for cardiac function under stress.

Science funders and research organizations in Europe are joining forces to expand open-access publishing and make the peer-review process more transparent, with the aim of spurring change in scholarly communication.
By early November, the European Commission will roll out an expanded version of its Open Research Europe (ORE) platform, which uses a ‘publish, review, curate’ model. In this approach, preprints are posted, reviewed openly — with the identity of the reviewers and their reports made public — then flagged as ‘peer reviewed’ on the same platform.
Joining the ORE are funders from 11 countries, including the German Research Foundation DFG and the Swiss National Science Foundation, as well as three major research organizations, including the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). More than 2.5 million researchers will now receive full editorial services on the platform at no charge. Since its launch in 2021, ORE has published some 1,500 articles.
“This is a collective effort to build a more transparent, sustainable publishing system that serves the research community and society as a whole,” says Karla Anaya-Carlsson, who chairs the ORE Funders Group and is based in Stockholm.
A big burden?
Mario Malički, a metascientist at Stanford University in California, says that the platform simplifies publishing for researchers and reduces funders’ costs. But, he cautions, running something at that scale “becomes a major undertaking of who runs the checks, who curates it and makes the final decisions”.
The expanded project has a budget of €16 million (US$17.7 million) between now and 2030, 60% of which will be provided by the European Commission and the remainder coming from the other funders and research organizations. It will be governed by these bodies, and hosted and operated by CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland.
Independently of the expansion of ORE, a group of 40 funders, institutions, publishers and platforms announced on 28 October the creation of the Publish, Review, Curate Alliance to promote such open publishing initiatives. Members include the journal eLife, the preprint organization OpenRxiv and the archiving service Europe PubMed Central. Other members include funders such as the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Gates Foundation, and institutional libraries at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and the University of Cambridge, UK.
Within two years of adopting this model, eLife lost its impact factor. Some bibliographic databases, including Web of Science, changed the way the journal was indexed. The finer details of how indexing services will respond to the expansion of ORE are not yet clear; ORE also has no impact factor, nor will it seek one.

articles.title: These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03325-3As poor publishing practices proliferate, scholarly databases are under pressure to ensure the titles they list are reputable.

Researchers have identified three warning signs that suggest journals might be engaging in suspicious publishing activities. Using these, they have found dozens of titles indexed in the leading scholarly database Scopus that could be problematic.
The three red flags are, for any given journal in a single year: a doubling of publication output; having more than 70% of published articles originating from a single country; and having at least 15% of articles flagged by the Problematic Paper Screener, a free online tool.
Using titles extracted from the freely available database OpenAlex, the researchers identified 3,753 journals that met at least one of these criteria. They cross-referenced these with journals indexed in Scopus and found that, of those, 5% had been delisted. The findings were published in a preprint1 on 20 October.
The researchers, and research-integrity specialists, say that the signals help to identify journals that merit further investigation — but do not prove that titles are problematic. They serve as “rudimentary flags”, says Achal Agrawal, a co-author of the preprint and a freelance data scientist in Raipur, India. And they indicate the problems that databases face as poor publishing practices proliferate, he adds.
Rankings basis
Bibliometric databases such as Scopus are important in the global research ecosystem because they inform many rankings used to evaluate individual researchers and institutions. Inclusion in Scopus, run by the Dutch publisher Elsevier, typically indicates that a journal is reputable.
Scopus regularly reviews the journals it lists, using a tool to spot signs of suspicious activities that suggest titles are churning out low-quality research that doesn’t adhere to accepted scholarly standards. These include “changes in publication volume and journal scope, unusual patterns in authorship and author collaboration, anomalous citation behaviour, and indications that a journal has become vulnerable to questionable content”, a spokesperson for Elsevier told Nature.
For flagged journals, Scopus then conducts “a careful, individual assessment of all available information, including consideration of the journal’s own response”, the spokesperson added. It removes journals that do not meet certain metrics thresholds. Scopus delisted 156 journals last year, and has removed 100 so far this year.
“No single signal, and no fixed threshold, determines the outcome,” Elsevier’s spokesperson said. “A signal is a prompt to investigate, and where needed the journal is put forward for re-evaluation” by Scopus’s content-selection board.
The study reported that the roughly 3,500 journals that have not been delisted together contributed more than half a million papers in the years that they were flagged by at least one signal. Nearly 300 journals were flagged by two signals and 28 journals by all three.
Each signal warrants a further look into the journal, but on its own is not “a definite decision to delist”, says Anna Abalkina, a research-integrity sleuth and social scientist at the Free University of Berlin. “There could be a lot of reasons why a journal duplicates the volume of publication.” For example, that often happens for a new journal, or as part of a publisher’s business plan, she says. But Abalkina thinks that a journal with all three red flags suggests suspicious activity that is difficult to find legitimate justification for.
Álvaro Cabezas Clavijo, who studies research evaluation at the International University of La Rioja in Logroño, Spain, agrees that the three signs should be interpreted with care. For instance, for small journals, having a large proportion of papers from one country might not be “a mark of questionable practices”.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03476-3A marked rise in submissions for the European Research Council’s grants is pushing down success rates.

A 60% growth in applications to one of the world’s most prestigious research-grant programmes could result in an exceptionally low success rate, raising fears that quality scientific ideas will go unfunded. This rise is attributable, in part, to the ease of writing applications with artificial-intelligence tools.
“The number is a bit scary,” says Maria Leptin, president of the European Research Council (ERC) in Brussels, noting that it’s increasingly difficult for their staff and peer reviewers to tackle so many applications.
The ERC’s Starting Grant programme — which offers base funds of up to €1.5 million (US$1.7 million) over five years to early-career scientists — received 7,710 proposals for 2027 grants before the deadline on 14 October, up from 4,807 last year (see ‘Rising torrent’).
With up to 373 grants available, down from 421 last year because of funding constraints, that will mean a success rate of less than 5%, compared with 8.8% for the 2026 grant call. “It’s almost a lottery,” says Devang Mehta, a systems and synthetic biologist at the Catholic University of Leuven in Belgium who applied for a Starting Grant this year.
Submissions rocket
The ERC is the Europe Union’s elite funder of basic research, and has an annual budget of nearly €3 billion. It offers three grant categories — Starting, Consolidator and Advanced — for individual researchers at growing stages of seniority. All have seen significant increases in applications in recent years.
Similar rises in research-grant applications are happening worldwide, says Lynn Kamerlin, a molecular biologist at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta who has studied grant success rates1. An ideal success rate for grant programmes is about 20%, she says. Any lower and it becomes increasingly difficult to select the best research without subjective judging, meaning that a lot of good science will go unfunded, she adds. “People can’t tell the difference between the top 6, 8, 12%.”
She suggests that one solution is to have a panel select the top 20% of applications and then pick winners at random, as some funders are doing. Anything below that threshold “is a lottery anyhow”, she says.
The rise in submissions has been attributed in part to artificial intelligence making it simpler to write grant applications. “It’s just so much easier to generate text,” says Kamerlin. That’s putting huge pressure on the system, she says, because “it can spin absolute nonsense”, meaning that reviews of applications require greater scrutiny.

Infecting people with a weak strain of dengue virus is helping researchers to unravel the disease’s bizarre effects on the immune system.
Dengue is spread when someone is bitten by an infected female Aedes mosquito. The viral disease kills around 40,000 people every year, with up to 400 million infected annually. Bangladesh and Kenya are among the countries battling a deadly outbreak. Although most adults survive their first brush with the disease, people who are exposed to a second, different strain of dengue virus often develop more severe symptoms.
This unusual quirk has complicated dengue vaccine development. Now, a human challenge trial that exposed 45 people to a modified mild strain of dengue virus is beginning to reveal the immunological underpinnings of dengue’s second wind, according to a study published in Science Translational Medicine on 28 October1.
Understanding the biology behind dengue’s infection pattern could help researchers to develop better vaccines, says study co-author Leah Katzelnick, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in Bethesda, Maryland.
“Dengue is still considered a neglected tropical disease,” she says. “But it’s become a problem for almost everyone now.”
Part of the problem with existing dengue vaccines is that even the immunizations can trigger secondary infections. This issue caused concern in the Philippines when some children contracted severe dengue infections after a major public vaccination effort started there in 2016.
A dangerous memory
Why the secondary infections happen is unclear. One theory is that, when confronted with a different dengue virus strain, the immune system deploys antibodies that were originally generated against the previous dengue strain it encountered. These antibodies aren’t as effective against the second strain, which can lead to people experiencing worse symptoms. Subsequent infections with other variants of dengue don’t seem to trigger the same immune response.
To learn more about how dengue immunology works, Katzelnick and her colleagues recruited 45 healthy people and split them into three groups: those who had never been infected with dengue; others who had been infected by one dengue virus strain; and those who had been infected by several dengue strains. The team then exposed all participants to a weakened version of DENV-3 (one of four strains of the virus) and compared their immune responses using blood and lymph-node samples.

You go to see a psychiatrist a decade from now. Alongside the usual questions about how you’re feeling, your work and your relationships, they look at biometric data from your phone about your sleep and speech patterns, examine the results of a blood test or a brain scan and even check your postcode to see whether your neighbourhood has high levels of pollution. An algorithm then compares that information with data from thousands of other people, determines which types of treatment have worked best for people similar to you and uses its findings to suggest a treatment regime.
That’s a vision of the future called precision psychiatry. And it’s a world away from most people’s experiences today. For all the progress that has been made across the medical sciences, psychiatry remains a frustratingly imprecise discipline. Doctors use someone’s symptoms and clinical history to make a diagnosis and prescribe treatments. But mental-health diagnoses are broad and can be vague — a particular therapy might transform one person’s life, but offer little help to someone else with apparently the same disorder.
As a result, people with mental-health conditions often find themselves cycling through treatments and doses, searching, mostly by trial and error, for one that works.
To improve things, psychiatrists want to divide broad diagnoses into more useful subgroups and match treatments to individuals using a data-driven approach. Some researchers are looking at genes and brain circuits; others are turning to data on speech, sleep or social circumstances. Psychiatrists working on TheDiagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the discipline’s dominant classification system, are even considering how socio-economic, cultural and environmental factors might be incorporated in the future.
“I think precision psychiatry is certainly part of the future,” says Tom Insel, a psychiatrist and former director of the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), who now co-directs several mental-health-focused companies. “We’ll be able to say from the get-go, this patient needs this treatment and that’s where they’re going to do best.”
But some clinicians say that the personalized approach has yet to prove itself. Advances in genetics, brain imaging and biomarker research for psychiatry have failed to deliver on their promise before, and studies continue to reveal just how heterogeneous many psychiatric disorders are. “Psychiatry has this model that the white knight is going to ride over the hill and solve all our problems,” says Kenneth Kendler, a psychiatric geneticist at Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond. “And we’ve been repeatedly disappointed.”
Classifying with precision
Personalized psychiatry is a catchy phrase, but it’s not a new idea.
Psychiatry has been trying to add precision to diagnosis and treatment for decades. In 1980, the third edition of the DSM introduced specific diagnostic criteria for many conditions. The aim was to boost reliability: a diagnosis of major depression or schizophrenia should mean roughly the same thing for everyone, even when issued by different psychiatrists.
But the DSM relies on symptoms to define conditions, and that proxy introduces complexities. The same symptoms appear in many conditions, and one person might have several diagnoses. Moreover, two people who have been diagnosed with the same condition can manifest it in quite different ways.
To meet DSM criteria for major depressive disorder, for example, a person must, in a two-week period, experience at least five symptoms out of a list of nine. The five must include a depressed mood or a loss of interest or pleasure; the remaining criteria include insomnia or excessive sleep, weight loss or gain, feelings of guilt or worthlessness and suicidal thoughts.
“It’s possible to have two people have the same diagnosis without a single required symptom in common,” says Vikram Patel, a psychiatrist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts.
By the late 2000s, researchers were increasingly questioning whether the approved disease categories were the best way to classify and treat people.
At the NIMH, Insel helped to develop the Research Domain Criteria initiative, which tried to go beyond categories and instead study and measure processes such as reward, fear and cognition, which cut across diagnostic boundaries. The idea encouraged researchers to study behaviours and brain functions that are shared across conditions. Although the programme has helped to shift research towards the underlying mechanisms of illness, it was never intended to replace the symptoms-based diagnostic system, and it does not provide a reliable way to select treatments for individuals.
Another approach to precision is to measure someone’s symptoms and behaviour with more rigour. A psychiatrist assessing psychosis, for example, listens to a person and judges qualities such as coherence, paranoia and grandiosity. That relies on human expertise, but also introduces human subjectivity.
Insel imagines a machine-learning system listening to the same person speaking and assigning more objective, reproducible measurements. “The paranoia score here is 6.1,” he suggests. “The coherence level is 2.2.”
John Torous, a psychiatrist at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Centre in Boston and at Harvard Medical School, works on a related approach known as digital phenotyping, in which information from smartphones and wearable sensors is used to study behaviour. The term emerged around a decade ago, when researchers proposed that sensors already carried around in smartphones could provide continuous measures of various behaviours, such as physical mobility and communication, that could inform diagnosis1.
Small studies have since found links between activity levels and depressive and manic symptoms in bipolar disorder2, and between location data and symptom severity in schizophrenia3.
The difficulty has been turning these data into something that is useful in the clinic. Medical education has not generally trained clinicians to interpret this information, Torous says, and researchers have not yet developed standards and protocols for using it. “So, we are in the early days in that sense.”
Artificial intelligence could make the difference, he suggests, because it can analyse a range of data streams and package them into useful clinical information.
The approach does come with concerns about privacy: personal data on location, movement, sleep and communication can hold intimate information and could even be used to identify individuals. Furthermore, a systematic review published this year4 found that digital-phenotyping studies showed wide variation in terms of the devices and analytical approaches they used. This could limit their reproducibility and potential for clinical translation.
Biological markers
Digging into biology more deeply could offer another route to precision. As genetics and neuroscience continue to advance, some researchers hope that the insights they provide will help to separate broad psychiatric syndromes into distinct diseases, with different underlying biological mechanisms and, eventually, different treatments.
This hasn’t happened yet, and some argue that it’s a futile exercise. Whereas biological insights helped researchers to divide diabetes into two separate types nearly a century ago, “we’ve never approached that in psychiatry”, says Kendler. Mental-health conditions could be “heterogeneous a long way down”.
Still, genetics has managed to produce one of psychiatry’s more promising potential biomarkers. By looking at the genomes of thousands of people with schizophrenia, in a type of study called genome-wide association, researchers have gleaned some idea about which gene variants confer risk.
For most health conditions, it is the combined small effects of many variants that add up to susceptibility. Geneticists call this collective estimate of risk a polygenic risk score. People towards the top of the polygenic-risk distribution for schizophrenia, says Kendler, can have around a tenfold increase in risk, although the size of the relative increase varies depending on the study. Published estimates5, for example, put risk at about six times higher for the top 1% than for everyone else. But the scores cannot predict who will develop a condition.
“Is it at such a stage now that I would get that score and immediately change what I’m doing diagnostically? No,” Kendler says.
In five or ten years, he says, it is conceivable that a score distinguishing schizophrenia from bipolar disorder could help in a difficult case in which the distinction would affect treatment.
Researchers have also investigated levels of hormones and metabolites as psychiatric biomarkers. But Kendler says that such measures have “almost always” proved to be non-specific. An average biological difference between groups is hard to translate into a specific test that can flag what is wrong with a particular person, or which treatment to offer.
Brain imaging offers another version of the same problem. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have reported large numbers of associations between features of the brain and psychiatric symptoms, but many of these have been difficult to reproduce.
A 2022 analysis6 of around 50,000 people found that associations between behavioural or mental-health traits and differences in brain structure or function were generally much smaller than previous studies had suggested.

Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
Some say the concept is complete fantasy, but a detailed analysis suggests that the falling cost of rocket launches might make it feasible in a few decades.
In August, entrepreneur Elon Musk suggested in a social-media post that Earth could be cooled by launching satellites into space to shade the planet from the Sun. These “sentient satellites”, he wrote, “can solve global warming for ~1B years”.
It’s unclear whether Musk, chief executive of the aerospace firm SpaceX in Starbase, Texas, meant for this to be taken seriously. But some researchers are earnestly investigating space-based methods of reflecting sunlight away from Earth to cool the planet as temperatures rise to increasingly dangerous levels.
A non-profit organization called the Planetary Sunshade Institute in Los Angeles, California, published a report this month that researchers say is the most detailed analysis yet of such geoengineering methods. The report — which summarizes studies from a consortium of engineers and climate scientists, including some from leading space agencies such as NASA — estimates that it could become viable to begin building a ‘planetary sunshade’ in as few as 20–40 years. The timeline would depend on the rate at which heavy-lift rockets are developed that can haul millions of tonnes of material into deep space to create the sunshade. (SpaceX, which is not involved in the report, did not respond to a query from Nature about whether it is conducting research on this topic.)
A lot of people think this idea is “just fantasy”, says Chantal Cappelletti, a space-systems engineer at the University of Nottingham, UK, who is part of the consortium. But the falling cost of space launches have made the prospect seem more feasible, she says.
Not so science fiction
Blocking sunlight to cool the planet through solar geoengineering has long been controversial. Proposals have included releasing sunlight-reflecting particles into Earth’s atmosphere, which could affect the planet in poorly understood ways, such as disrupting precipitation and plant growth. Space-based approaches could come with unique risks, including the pollution unleashed from many thousands of rocket launches. Critics also say that focusing attention on geoengineering distracts from the urgent need to cut greenhouse-gas emissions to address climate change.
But solar geoengineering has received more attention from researchers as Earth looks set to hurtle past 1.5 °C of warming above the planet’s pre-industrial baseline temperature. The “accelerating climate crisis” is pushing the world towards solar geoengineering, says Morgan Goodwin, a climate activist and executive director of the Planetary Sunshade Institute.
The report is the group’s biggest project so far, funded by a £400,000 (US$530,000) grant from the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a body sponsored by the government to fund high-risk, high-reward research. That grant is part of a larger £56.8-million ARIA research programme on solar geoengineering.
Daniele Visioni, a climate scientist at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, says that he had previously dismissed space-based approaches as science fiction. But after attending an engineering workshop on such approaches earlier this year, he was persuaded that they deserve more attention. However, “I still wouldn’t put this as something feasible before the end of the century”, he says.

Trust in science and researchers has fallen following the COVID-19 pandemic, the largest survey of public confidence in science shows. Led by the global biomedical funder Wellcome in London and published on 10 October, it explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence (see ‘Trust in decline’).
“We should be paying attention to, and thinking about, what needs to be done to earn that trust,” says Philippa Michael, head of public initiatives at Wellcome, who led the project. This is the third survey of its kind conducted by Wellcome, following editions in 2018 and 2020.
The analysis points to a “mixed” picture that varies between countries and regions, says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia (see ‘Regional differences’).
The study also shows a connection between science and people’s broader experiences, including their perceived financial security, says Michael (see ’Money matters‘).
“If people feel economically insecure, then they’re going to feel a greater distance between themselves and science and scientists,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat, at Harvard Kennedy School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This disconnect “is not about science’s efficacy or its ability to fix problems”, he adds.
The survey found that countries where people reported high confidence in hospitals and health-care clinics were “more likely to have greater trust in science”, notes Michael. Levels of trust were also high in respondents who were confident in accessing health-care services when needed. “It’s really essential that science is credible, relevant and beneficial to people in their lives,” Michael adds.

Holding her lunch box, Lili scanned the noon break area at the Exotic Destinations travel show. The middle-aged travel agents chattering among themselves ignored her, but a tall Black woman with snow-white hair waved.
Recognizing her from the session on tourism on the Extraterrestrial Highway, Lili walked over to ask, “May I join you?”
“Certainly,” the woman said. “My name’s Bettye, with an e at the end. I noticed you at the Extraterrestrial Highway session.”
“I’m Lili, with two l’s, two i’s and no y at all, and I saw you there. What did you think of their space alien experience?” She sat down to unpack her lunch.
“It’s changed tremendously since I was young,” Bettye said. “My parents just hoped to see a flying saucer on a long trip across the southwestern desert. Now they have cheesy roadside attractions with animated space aliens waving outside the door.”
Intrigued, Lili asked “What was it like back then?”
Read more science fiction from Nature Futures
“Flying saucers were a mystery in the sixties; everybody wanted to see one. Papa was an Air Force mechanic, and pilots told him they had seen saucers. The Byrds sung about hitching a ride on a saucer. Papa always looked for saucers.”
“Do your stories help sell tours?” Lili asked.
“It helps sell tours on Route 66.”
“I wish I had travel stories, but my parents were too poor to take vacations after they immigrated from Hong Kong.”
Bettye grinned. “Oh, we loved telling those stories about looking for flying saucers, but we had to be careful we didn’t scare anyone.”
“Oh …” Lili said, trying to lead her on.
Bettye sipped her iced tea and sat back. “I saw my first saucer when we were driving through the desert. Papa drove at night because our old station wagon didn’t have air conditioning. The Moon was bright so we could see the foothills and the cacti. I fell asleep, but woke when Papa stopped. He and Mama whispered and pointed at a moonlit saucer parked a little ways away. A hatch opened and two aliens got out and walked towards us. Mama said we better go, but the car wouldn’t start. The aliens wore pale green suits and carried metal boxes that looked like old telephones. I waved, and they waved back.”
“Were you scared?”
“A little,” Bettye said. “Then the boxes started talking English voices like we heard on the radio. Mama hushed me when I giggled.”
“What did they say?”
“They asked us to fly them over the mountains and tell them about the scenery. Papa laughed and said our car couldn’t fly. They said theirs could, and Mama got them to pay us to guide them. Mama was scared because she had never flown, but Papa and I had a great flight. After we landed, the aliens asked if we would guide other aliens on trips.”
“Did you?”
“Oh yes. Papa took me along and we had a great time guiding the alien tours. They were very friendly and what they paid let me go to college.”
“That was a very successful business,” Lili said. “How long did it last?”
Bettye nodded. “Several years, until a saucer flew too close to an Air Force base. A pilot at the base jumped into a fighter and flew towards us. Papa told the aliens to fly away because the fighter might shoot us down, but their speaking boxes said ‘no civilized beings would do that’.”
“What happened?”
“The fighter shot a missile at us. Then one alien pointed something at the missile and it vanished. The other alien pointed a box at the plane and made it move with what he called a force field. He made it land on the road. The pilot opened the door and ran away while we watched the alien melt the plane.”

Early-career researchers are well aware of the uncertainties that an academic career can bring. Nevertheless, many expect that if they remain in academia, their careers will progress in a relatively familiar way: after completing a doctorate, they will move into a postdoctoral position, establish research independence, obtain a permanent post and, eventually, enter a more settled stage of academic life.
The conversations that my colleagues and I have had with established researchers while working on the White Rose Established Researchers project — a collaboration between the UK universities of Leeds, Sheffield and York that aims to support career development — suggest that career progression is often much less linear.
Research independence, which is characterized as a researcher’s ability to lead and sustain an original programme of research, is typically associated with the mid-career stage in academia. It brings with it a fresh set of challenges: how to sustain research while leading people, managing competing responsibilities and prioritizing the tasks that can have the greatest impact. The researchers whom we interviewed rarely spoke about having ‘made it’; instead, they described having to regularly refresh and revise how they think about their careers, in circumstances of increasing uncertainty.
It is striking how little attention has been paid to understanding the period between establishing research independence and the later stages of an academic career. Universities have invested heavily in supporting early-career researchers and have developed sophisticated programmes for senior leaders. Yet, relatively little attention has been given to the distinctive experiences of academics occupying the space between those career stages.
Our collaboration explored how established researchers experience the middle stage of their career. Across four months, we interviewed 27 established researchers, held two focus groups with them, sent them a follow-up survey to validate our findings and mapped institutional resources across the three universities.
Because no widely accepted definition of an established researcher exists, we defined them as “an academic who has achieved functional independence and institutional recognition in their research capacity, whilst continuing to develop their professional identity and navigate complex career transitions”.
The established-researcher career stage is characterized by a distinct research agenda, the capacity to secure and manage funding, a strong track record of scholarly outputs, recognition in relevant research communities and the ability to make substantive intellectual contributions to their field.
The common experience: juggling complexity
Across disciplines, established researchers described a shared experience of juggling various, often competing, responsibilities that span research, teaching, leadership, administration and collaboration. The challenge was rarely any individual role; instead, it was the continual negotiation of priorities across them.
As we analysed the interviews, we found that researchers were making sense of this complexity in different ways. To help to illuminate these recurring patterns, we outlined four personas that can be used to articulate different approaches to navigating the established stage of an academic career.
No researcher fits perfectly into a single persona. Many recognized aspects of themselves in more than one and described moving between them over time. But we developed these personas to understand how researchers think about success, make decisions and respond to the continuing complexity of academic life.
The laboratory builder
For some established researchers, academic life revolves around people as much as projects. Alongside developing their own research programmes, they recruit and train staff, secure funding and create opportunities for others. Many described an important transition from being the person who mainly conducts research to becoming the one who galvanizes the collective efforts of a team to enable research to happen.
For anyone hoping to lead a research group, this persona offers an important reminder: independence entails leadership, delegation, shaping research culture and balancing investment in others with maintenance of your own scientific expertise. Many researchers described the challenge of redefining success as their role shifted from doing research themselves to enabling the work of others. What got them to this point in their career was not always what was required to succeed in the next stage. This work is not routinely celebrated, yet it is fundamental to the long-term success of many research environments.
The independent scholar
Many early-career researchers assume that becoming established means leading ever-larger groups. However, independent scholars organize their careers around sustained intellectual contribution: their influence comes from the ideas they develop and the scholarship they produce, pushing forwards thinking in their discipline. They might collaborate widely, but their work is characterized less by organizational expansion than by continuity of intellectual purpose.
One of their greatest challenges is protecting the quality thinking time that sustained scholarship requires while juggling the pressures of increasingly fragmented academic roles. Many also described the challenge of gaining recognition for forms of contribution that do not depend on large-scale grant funding, including editorial work, intellectual leadership and the development of scholarly communities that stimulate fresh debates and directions for research.
The project architect
Some established researchers described careers centred on leading collaborative research on a large scale. Whether coordinating multidisciplinary teams, cross-institutional partnerships or large funded programmes, they bring together people, expertise and opportunities across several projects that do not necessarily form a single coherent research programme. Rather than building one permanent team, these researchers create successive collaborations that evolve as ideas, funding opportunities and partnerships emerge.
Their biggest challenge is maintaining a coherent sense of purpose while managing numerous projects, partnerships and opportunities simultaneously. As their portfolio grows, deciding which opportunities to pursue and which to decline becomes an increasingly important part of their professional development.

articles.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11180-5A geoarchaeological survey of the Rub’ al Khali (the Empty Quarter of Arabia) and spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula suggest that human settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and stone suitable for making tools, rather than water alone.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography1,2, particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior3.
Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained4,5, a pattern not explained by water availability alone.
Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement.
Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins.
Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone.
Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.
695 to 0.
768.
Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia.
Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

Main
Predictive models of early human dispersal across Arabia, built primarily on palaeohydrological reconstructions of palaeolake and palaeoriver networks and on climate-envelope reconstructions of precipitation and net primary productivity, identify interior basins as high-probability zones for Middle Palaeolithic (MP) and Middle Stone Age (MSA) occupation3,6, the broadly contemporaneous prepared-core industries of western Eurasia and Africa, respectively; because Arabian assemblages show affinities with both, the joint term MP/MSA is used throughout. The expectation that these palaeolakes attracted human settlement reflects decades of palaeoclimatic research demonstrating that orbital forcing periodically transformed the Arabian Peninsula into landscapes of lakes, wetlands and grasslands7,8,9. Geographical Information System (GIS)-based models built on this record have shown predictive success at the Rub’ al Khali margins, where dated MP/MSA assemblages occur alongside lacustrine deposits in the western basin10,11. Yet these models have never been verified against systematic ground survey in the desert interior, nor have they been evaluated against the distribution of knappable raw materials, a resource fundamental to Palaeolithic subsistence12 and consumed at rates that varied with the technology used13,14. Although it has been recognized that water would not be the sole determining factor in site location6, no study has evaluated this other variable.
The Rub’ al Khali occupies around 650,000 km2 of the southern Arabian Peninsula, bounded by the Asir and Yemen highlands to the west, the Dhofar Nejd and Hadhramaut plateaus to the south, the Hajar Mountains to the east and the Tuwaiq escarpment and Ad Dahna desert to the north. Its interior is dominated by longitudinal dune systems separated by interdunal corridors in which Quaternary sediments are exposed by deflation. During Pleistocene humid intervals, precession-driven intensification of the Indian Ocean monsoon raised regional water tables and formed lakes across the basin7,8,9,15, the most extensive of which are documented for Marine Isotope Stage 516. Archaeological evidence for these intervals is concentrated at the desert margins, where MP/MSA assemblages occur alongside dated lacustrine deposits at Mundafan10,11, Jebel Faya17,18, Umm al Sha’al19 and the Dhofar Nejd Plateau5,20. These assemblages are technologically diverse: Levallois and other prepared-core reduction strategies predominate, with Nubian Levallois industries of African affinity documented in the south20,21 and assemblages of western Asian character in the north4. The interior basin itself, however, has never been surveyed systematically and its archaeological status has been inferred from the margins rather than tested.
To test the prediction that interior basins were high-probability zones for MP/MSA occupation, a systematic geoarchaeological reconnaissance of the desert interior was conducted along an approximately 1,500-km transect through the central Rub’ al Khali (Fig. 1). The survey targeted palaeolake deposits correlated to sections independently dated to about 122,000–67,000 years ago16, focusing on the MP/MSA. This period corresponds to both the dated palaeolake chronologies and documented Homo sapiens dispersals into Arabia17,20,22. Because the nearest known knappable outcrops lie more than 200 km from the surveyed basins, the interior decouples water from stone. This study therefore tests whether the co-occurrence of freshwater and knappable stone, rather than freshwater alone, accounts for the distribution of archaeologically visible MP/MSA occupation in the Arabian interior. If freshwater alone governed settlement, MP/MSA populations occupying the adjacent margins would be expected to have left archaeologically visible traces in the interior during humid phases. Abundant evidence for palaeolakes was recorded, but no knappable raw materials, no lithic artefacts and no trace of human occupation were found. An independent spatial model, validated against 301 MP/MSA findspots in adjacent Oman, indicates that settlement was concentrated in zones where both water and raw materials co-occurred; a Peninsula-wide analysis shows the same pattern across 363 documented MP/MSA sites.
Spatial modelling
Human occupation potential across the Arabian Peninsula was modelled from mapped surface geology and reconstructed drainages. This dual-resource model was initially tested in Oman, where systematic survey allowed for estimating the likelihood of raw-material availability. The model shows that occupation potential is concentrated in narrow zones where both water and knappable raw materials co-occur, predominantly along the Dhofar Nejd and western Hajar piedmont, whereas interior regions score low despite their proximity to water (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Known MP/MSA sites cluster overwhelmingly in these highest-potential zones (Extended Data Fig. 1d), consistent with settlement tracking the co-occurrence of water and knappable stone, rather than water alone (Supplementary Fig. 7). The same pattern emerges at the Peninsula-wide scale (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 2); of the total area of the Arabian Peninsula within water-proximity thresholds, 57% lies on geological formations that lack knappable lithologies.
Field survey
The expedition investigated 125 localities along the survey transect, of which 55 yielded palaeolake deposits (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2).
The eastern localities lie among sections independently dated by luminescence to Marine Isotope Stage 5, between about 122 thousand years ago (ka) and 67 ka (ref.
16).
Contemporary occupation is documented at the Rub’ al Khali margins at Mundafan (about 96–77 ka)10,11, Umm al Sha’al (about 87–71 ka)19, Jebel Faya (about 134–80 ka)17,18,23 and the Dhofar Nejd plateau (about 109–95 ka)5,20 (Fig.
1b, Supplementary Table 4 and Supplementary Information, section 6).
Freshwater lakes and nearby populations therefore seem to have overlapped regionally across this interval, yet the surveyed interior produced no archaeologically visible occupation evidence.
Carbonate lacustrine sediments, ostrich eggshell fragments, and freshwater mollusc assemblages dominated by Melanoides tuberculata and Corbicula fluminalis were observed at palaeolake localities (Fig.
3).
Sedimentological features, including bioturbated limestones, dolomitic microbial build-ups, gypsum rosettes indicative of terminal desiccation and trace fossils characteristic of shallow lacustrine environments, are consistent with previous palaeoenvironmental interpretations.
These waterbodies ranged from freshwater at highstand, indicated by the mollusc and limestone facies, to saline during desiccation.
More localities were recorded at equivalent elevations to the deposits investigated by ref.
16 and represent fragmented remnants of the same palaeolake systems (Extended Data Fig.
3 and Supplementary Information, section 3).

The transect started at isolated outcrops of Jurassic Hanifa Formation, which provided lithic raw material for the MP/MSA occupation at nearby Mundafan10,11.
Approximately 80 km further northeast, the last bedrock outcrops were documented (Lower Cretaceous Wasia Formation); these yielded heavily weathered silicified sandstones, of limited suitability for stone tool manufacture (sites 8 and 9; Supplementary Information, section 1).
East of these outcrops, the chert-bearing Mesozoic–Eocene formations dip beneath a thick sequence of Miocene to Quaternary siliciclastic, carbonatic and evaporitic sediments.
In the central Rub’ al Khali, only small, isolated remnants of these younger basin-fill deposits are exposed between dune fields and none contains knappable lithologies (Fig.
4).
Despite systematic reconnaissance and high ground visibility, no lithic artefacts or other cultural materials were recorded at any surveyed locality and no lithic raw materials were found throughout the transect, whether as exposed bedrock or transported clasts, except at its westernmost and easternmost ends.
Knappable stone was confined to 10 of 125 localities (8%): two Wasia Formation outcrops in the west and eight eastern-margin localities comprising one Dammam Formation bedrock exposure and seven alluvial gravel deposits carrying reworked chert.

articles.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11211-1A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2.
Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3,4,5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear.
Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC.
Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy.
We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C.
perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury.
Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation.
Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin.
Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C.
perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis.
Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression.
These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

Main
NEC remains a major cause of mortality and long-term morbidity in preterm infants1,2. NEC pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving the complex interplay of immature intestinal development, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut dysbiosis and excessive inflammatory response3,4,5,6. The specific triggers of NEC and the mechanisms driving its rapid progression remain poorly understood.
The impact of NEC extends beyond the intestine. More than half of postoperative survivors develop brain injury and neurodevelopmental impairment7,8, with TLR4 inflammatory pathways implicated in this pathology9,10. Many insights are derived from experimental models that use hypoxia, cold stress and hyperosmolar formula feeding to increase intestinal vulnerability11,12. Although these models have been valuable for mapping inflammatory pathways, they may be less well suited to interrogating microbiome-driven early initiating events.
Gut microbiota are implicated in NEC susceptibility: NEC is associated with dysbiosis3,4,5, germ-free mice are resistant to NEC-like injury13 and microbiota-modifying interventions are protective14,15. Several studies identified enrichment of toxin-producing C. perfringens in NEC16,17,18, but causal virulence factors remain undefined.
C. perfringens is a ubiquitous, Gram-positive anaerobe producing diverse toxins19,20. Strains are classified into seven toxin types (A–G) based on toxin repertoire19. Type C strains produce Beta and Delta toxins, which are both pore-forming toxins (PFTs) that induce cell death by forming transmembrane pores21,22,23. While Beta toxin is well characterized, Delta toxin remains understudied. Here we identify C. perfringens Delta toxin as a virulence factor that drives intestinal necrosis and brain injury in a subset of NEC, providing an avenue for targeted therapeutic intervention.
Delta toxin+ C. perfringens marks severe NEC
To investigate the role of gut microbiota in NEC, we profiled faecal samples from 28 preterm infants without NEC and 16 preterm infants with NEC. 16S rRNA-sequencing analysis revealed an enrichment of C. perfringens in NEC samples (Fig. 1a), consistent with previous reports16,17. Two fatal cases of NEC showed high C. perfringens abundance (Extended Data Fig. 1a). To validate this finding, we performed anaerobic culture of faecal samples from 49 individuals without NEC and 17 patients with NEC (Supplementary Table 1). C. perfringens-positive cultures showed visible gas production and were confirmed by selective tryptose sulfite cycloserine (TSC) agar isolation and PCR targeting of C. perfringens-specific genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d). Overall, C. perfringens was more prevalent in patients with NEC compared with in infants without NEC (56% versus 18%), supporting its association with NEC (Fig. 1b,c).
C. perfringens produces a repertoire of toxins, including Alpha, Beta, Epsilon, Iota toxin, enterotoxin (CPE), necrotic enteritis β-like toxin (NetB) and perfringolysin O (Pfo)19. We next examined whether specific toxin profiles correlated with severe outcomes. PCR-based toxin typing identified isolates from two deceased patients as type C C. perfringens strains containing the delta toxin gene (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens clinical-03 and clinical-15) (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta toxin production was further confirmed by western blot analysis of culture supernatants (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). We further detected anti-Delta toxin antibodies in two patients with severe surgical NEC whose stool cultures were negative, probably due to antibiotic treatment, indicating previous infection with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens strains. Expanded serological analysis of ten additional patients with severe surgical NEC identified five anti-Delta toxin antibody-positive cases (Supplementary Table 2). Thus, 7 of 12 (58%) patients with severe NEC showed serological evidence of Delta toxin exposure, whereas Delta toxin was not detected in any infant without NEC by faecal isolate PCR or serology (Fig. 1b–d).
Clinically, Delta toxin+ infants showed more prominent systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and brain injury, compared with Delta toxin− cases characterized by elevated C-reactive protein and D-dimer, decreased monocytes, platelets and haemoglobin (Fig. 1e). Importantly, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in these patients indicated more severe injury, including lateral ventricular enlargement (Fig. 1f,g).
Delta toxin+ C. perfringens drives NEC-like pathology
To assess Delta toxin pathogenicity, we selected representative clinical isolates, the Delta toxin+ strain C.
perfringens clinical-03 and the Delta toxin− strain C.
perfringens clinical-01 for genomic analysis and animal infection studies (Extended Data Fig.
1e,f).
Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the clinical-03 strain clustered with NCTC3181 (a known Delta toxin+ type C strain24), whereas clinical-01 clustered with CVCC1160 (a Delta toxin− type C strain), with the two clinical isolates sharing around 96% DNA identity (Extended Data Fig.
1h).
Neonatal mice orally gavaged with these strains and formula for 4 days developed severe NEC-like intestinal pathology only after Delta toxin+ infection, including disrupted intestinal architecture, villus and crypt damage, inflammatory infiltration and mucosal fibrin clots, accompanied by increased mortality (Fig.
1h–k).
During infection with the clinical-03 strain, Delta toxin was detected predominantly in the intestine, with lower levels in the kidney and lung, but was undetectable in the brain based on western blotting and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Extended Data Fig.
1i,j).
Nevertheless, infected mice developed severe brain abnormalities, including lateral ventricular enlargement and ependymal cell damage (Fig.
1l,m).
Reference strain comparison using NCTC3181 and CVCC1160 (around 99% identity) confirmed that Delta toxin+ infection caused more severe intestinal, brain and lung injury (Extended Data Fig.
1k–m).
Finally, culture supernatants from Delta toxin+ strains induced cytotoxicity in HeLa cells, HT29 cells and intestinal organoids, which was neutralized by a Delta-toxin-specific polyclonal antibody (Extended Data Fig.
1n–p).
These results support Delta toxin as a key secreted virulence factor responsible for cell damage.

Owing to technical challenges in performing some assays in postnatal day 7 (P7) neonatal mice, we included 4-week-old weanling mice for subsequent experiments. Intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration of purified Delta toxin caused dose-dependent lethality in both age groups, with neonates showing greater sensitivity (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). Consistent with the infection model, toxin levels were highest in the intestine (around 61 μg per g), followed by kidney (approximately 15 μg per g) and lung (about 7 μg per g), with barely detectable toxin in the brain (Extended Data Fig. 2b). These levels were comparable to those in infected pups, supporting the physiological relevance of the toxin injection model.
We next challenged P7 neonates and 4-week-old mice using either an acute high-dose model to mimic fulminant infection, analysed at 4 h, or a single low-dose challenge with prolonged follow-up to approximate residual toxin activity after antibiotic clearance, analysed at days 5–7. Across both age groups and dosing strategies, Delta toxin induced a severe NEC-like multiorgan pathology. Intestines showed mucosal disruption, villus destruction, epithelial detachment and oedema (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). articles.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10438-2Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1.
Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.
4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.
7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression.
We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.
7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference.
Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.
4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture.
Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.
1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits.
Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation.

articles.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11195-yComputational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3,4,5,6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100—a known command neuron for walking—as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

articles.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11202-2Planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons are synthesized by laterally fusing polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains, suggesting a possible route towards carbon quantum wires.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4.
Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1.
However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored.
The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9,10,11,12,13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16,17,18,19,20.
Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains.
Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges.
CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor.
The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4.
This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration.

Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. articles.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11181-4Dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity1,2,3,4,5,6,7, but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear.
Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity.
This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification.
Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref.
8) and Il1b.
Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification.
These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1+CD4+ T helper type 17 (TH17) cells9,10.
After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists.
Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD.
Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung TH17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms.
Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.
