Main
Obesity alters immune function across multiple contexts, including infection, autoimmunity and cancer7,12,13,14,15,16,17. This effect is especially pronounced in the skin, where obesity exacerbates inflammation and complicates therapeutic responses6,18. Although chronic obesity and weeks to months of obesogenic diet exposure are known to remodel cutaneous immunity, these longer interventions also produce cumulative metabolic, endocrine, microbial and tissue remodelling across multiple organ systems7. It remains unclear whether comparatively brief, days-scale dietary exposures, before such systemic remodelling is established, can acutely modify triggered inflammatory responses and durably imprint long-term tissue inflammatory memory. Experimental models of acute type 17 skin inflammation provide an opportunity to examine these effects, as psoriasis, a type 17 inflammatory disease tightly linked to obesity4,15, has also been associated with dietary patterns and other nutritional exposures19,20,21. We therefore examined whether transient dietary state could bidirectionally modify the response to a synchronized inflammatory trigger, such that HFD amplifies inflammation in lean mice whereas LFD restrains inflammation in obese mice, and whether this acute dietary window could alter subsequent tissue inflammatory recall.
Diet, not body mass, dictates disease
To distinguish the impact of diet itself from the consequences of established obesity, we used topical imiquimod (IMQ) challenge as a synchronized model of acute type 17 skin inflammation in which age-matched mice were fed either a short-term (1 week) or long-term (10 weeks) HFD (60% kcal from fat), or a low-fat (control) diet (LFD; 10% kcal from fat), before topical IMQ challenge22 (Fig. 1a). Mice remained on their assigned diets throughout IMQ challenge. Measurements of serum cytokine levels before application of IMQ did not reveal significant differences between the three groups (Extended Data Fig. 1a), although we did observe modestly increased numbers of TH17 cells and γδ T cells in the skin of mice fed a short- and long-term HFD, relative to the mice fed LFD (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d). Both short- and long-term HFD also reduced glucose tolerance, although these effects were more pronounced in obese mice that were fed a long-term HFD (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b).
As expected, 10 weeks of HFD caused marked obesity, whereas HFD for 1 week did not (Fig. 1b). Despite this, both regimens exacerbated IMQ-induced skin inflammation comparably, with approximately 2.1-fold (1 week) and 2.3-fold (10 week) increases in ear thickness relative to the LFD-fed mice (Fig. 1c). Gross examination revealed equivalent levels of ear shortening (Fig. 1d), and histological analysis showed dermal and epidermal expansion in both groups (Fig. 1e). Notably, 1 week of feeding on a medium-fat diet (MFD; 45% kcal from fat) was sufficient to exacerbate disease to a similar extent to the HFD (60% kcal from fat) (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d), indicating that neither extreme fat exposure nor established obesity is required to amplify inflammation. Consistently, western diet (WD; 40 kcal% fat; 29 kcal% sucrose) feeding amplified inflammation after IMQ treatment to the same extent as MFD feeding (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Further, WD or HFD feeding alone did not induce overt ear inflammation or increased ear thickness in the absence of IMQ challenge across the time periods examined (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g), indicating that diet-sensitive amplification of IMQ-induced inflammation is experimentally separable from spontaneous diet-associated dermatitis as reported in some prolonged diet-feeding models23,24.
To determine whether systemic metabolic correction was sufficient to blunt diet-amplified inflammation, we treated HFD-fed mice with semaglutide during the acute dietary exposure and IMQ challenge. Semaglutide was pharmacologically active, improving glucose excursion, reducing body weight, lowering circulating insulin and leptin, increasing GLP-1 immunoreactivity in an assay that recognizes semaglutide, and reducing white adipose tissue mass (Extended Data Fig. 3a–h). However, semaglutide did not broadly reduce baseline inflammatory cytokines, alter gross ear or spleen morphology or substantially remodel splenic conventional T (Tconv) cell subsets (Extended Data Fig. 3i–l). After IMQ challenge, semaglutide did not attenuate HFD-amplified ear thickening or lesional TH17 inflammation (Extended Data Fig. 3m–p). Thus, HFD-conditioned inflammatory susceptibility can persist despite GLP-1 receptor agonist-mediated improvement in systemic metabolic parameters.
IMQ-induced inflammation predominantly stimulates type 17 immune responses, characterized by the production of IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 by TH17 cells, γδ T cells and other immune cells22,25. Flow cytometry revealed that acute and chronic HFD similarly increased levels of CD4+ Tconv cells expressing RORγt, the lineage-defining TH17 transcription factor, as well as CD4+ Tconv cells competent for IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 in lesional skin and draining lymph nodes (Extended Data Figs. 1b and 4a–d). TH22 cells (IL-17A−IL-22+FOXP3−CD4+ T cells) were also increased, although to a lesser extent than TH17 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4e). CD4+ T cell proliferation (Ki-67+) was increased (Extended Data Fig. 4f), whereas the proportion of Treg cells was reduced under both conditions (Extended Data Fig. 4g). Neutrophils, which are prominent cellular effectors of type 17 inflammation26, were elevated after just 1 week of HFD, mirroring the increase observed with chronic HFD (Extended Data Fig. 4h). By contrast, the proportion of cytokine-producing γδ T cells was unchanged, although total γδ T cell numbers increased in HFD-fed mice (Extended Data Fig. 4i,j).
Finally, we examined whether brief withdrawal of dietary fat could mitigate disease in obese mice. Mice fed HFD for 13 weeks were switched to LFD for 1 week before IMQ challenge, and were compared with obese mice maintained on HFD and with lean LFD-fed control mice (Fig. 1f). Despite persistent obesity (>40 g), the mice that were switched to LFD did not develop the enhanced ear thickness observed in obese mice maintained on HFD (Fig. 1g–j). Thus, dietary state at the onset of inflammation, rather than body mass alone, dictates the magnitude of inflammatory responses after acute challenge with IMQ. This result prompted us to test whether dietary exposure within a specific temporal window is sufficient to drive this effect.
A 4-day diet window sets severity
To define the temporal dynamics of this response, we examined how the timing of HFD feeding influenced IMQ-induced inflammation.
Four days of HFD coincident with disease initiation (HFDin) were sufficient to markedly exacerbate inflammation (Fig.
1k,l and Extended Data Fig.
4k,l).
Short-term exposure to 15% (w/v) glucose in water during the same peri-initiation window did not enhance IMQ-induced inflammation (Extended Data Fig.
2h–k), suggesting that increased simple sugar exposure is insufficient to recapitulate the acute inflammatory amplification observed with fat-enriched obesogenic diets.
By contrast, HFD provided outside this window (HFDout) did not alter disease severity compared with continuous LFD (Extended Data Fig.
2l).
Conversely, switching obese mice to LFD during a similar 4-day window (LFDin) protected them from the heightened inflammation observed in obese mice maintained on HFD (Fig.
1m,n), whereas LFD given outside this window (LFDout) offered no protection (Extended Data Fig.
2m).
In a complementary experiment, mice that were fed HFD for 1 week and switched to LFD on the day of IMQ initiation (HFDbefore) developed disease severity comparable to mice maintained on HFD, further narrowing the critical dietary window to the onset of inflammation (Extended Data Fig.
2n).
Together, these results establish that dietary state during the peri-initiation window, rather than obesity per se, determines disease severity, and raise the question of which immune compartments translate coincident dietary cues into amplified inflammatory responses.

articles.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11219-7In systemic lupus erythematosus, aberrant splicing in neutrophils generates novel peptides that are presented on MHC I, driving CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation, clonal expansion and IgG autoantibody responses, establishing neoantigen-driven autoimmune immunity.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing1. In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity2,3. Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

Main
SLE is a debilitating autoimmune disorder of unclear aetiology4,5,6. SLE involves multiple organs and is characterized by the presence of autoantibodies against nuclear proteins, nucleic acid-associated proteins and double-stranded DNA7. Although antigen-specific T cell responses8 have a substantial role, it is largely unknown what antigens the T cells respond to9. Mounting evidence also suggests that innate immune cells have a central role in driving the underlying mechanisms of SLE10,11,12,13,14, including the elevated levels of type I interferons found in most patients with SLE15. Neutrophils are increasingly implicated11,12,13,16,17,18 as sources of SLE autoantigens, including both nucleic acids and proteins, that are released during inflammatory cell death via processes such as NETosis13 and ferroptosis19. Although neutropoiesis is accelerated in SLE15, many patients are neutropenic, indicating increased neutrophil consumption. Neutrophils in SLE display widespread genomic hypomethylation, leading, in part, to a distinctive type I interferon-weighted transcriptional profile20, which differs from that in other autoimmune diseases, but bears much resemblance to that in neutrophils from SARS-CoV2-infected individuals21.
Alternative RNA transcript splicing begins during gene transcription and results in the nuclear export of mature mRNA variants that profoundly contribute to proteome complexity and molecular diversity1. Proteins that are translated from alternatively spliced mRNA often display substantial differences in molecular functions, stability and interactions with other proteins or nucleic acids. Alternative splicing can also modulate mRNA disposition, including degradation through nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)22. Alternative splicing occurs more frequently in autoantigen transcripts20 than in randomly selected proteins, and escape from NMD has been shown to cause autoimmunity23. Neutrophils represent an abundant reservoir of intracellular proteins and nucleic acids that potentially function as autoantigenic sources.
To comprehensively analyse alternative mRNA splicing, we created the RiboSplitter24 pipeline, which yields the translated protein products of splice variants. With this tool, we characterized 65,730 high-confidence alternative splicing events in 5,697 protein-coding genes in neutrophils from patients with SLE, of which 521 events in 356 genes were significantly different from healthy donors25. Here we focus on the SLE-restricted mRNA splicing events, referred to as ‘cryptic’ splicing events, that are predicted to generate novel protein sequences.
Cryptic splicing events in SLE neutrophils
Thirty-four patients with SLE, representing a typical academic medical centre population (Supplementary Table 1), consented to blood donation.
Healthy donors and patients with rheumatoid arthritis served as normal and disease controls, respectively.
Immune cells and neutrophils were isolated, and the patients’ sera were stored frozen until use.
RNA was isolated from neutrophils and used for stranded paired-end RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (Fig.
1a) to a sequencing depth of approximately 50 million reads with 101 bp read length (Fig.
1b).
We applied a minimum threshold of five reads to exclude stochastic low-frequency splicing artefacts, detecting a total of 271 cryptic splicing events in 130 genes in SLE neutrophils (n = 34), all of which were absent in neutrophils from the healthy donors (n = 20) and patients with rheumatoid arthritis (n = 15).
The most abundant events were abnormal exon skips, followed by multi-exon skips, atypical 5′ or 3′ splice sites and intron retention (Fig.
1c).
Several cryptic events were combinations of these mechanisms.
A pathway analysis of the aberrantly spliced genes showed a strong bias for type I interferon-inducible genes (Fig.
1d), including the most frequently mis-spliced genes IFI44L, MX1, OAS1, RSAD2, XAF1, IFI27, MX1 and IFIT1.
However, cryptic splicing events were also observed in genes that are not considered interferon-inducible, such as ABCG1, PSMF1 and OGG1 (Supplementary Fig.
1), indicating that expression level alone cannot explain the generation of these cryptic splicing events, although it could be a factor.
As expected, read support for cryptic splicing events was lower than for non-cryptic events (Fig.
1e), but read support for cryptic splicing events that generated novel peptide sequences varied from 283 reads down to our cut-off threshold of 5 (median = 10).

Cryptic splicing events were detected in 33 out of 34 patients with SLE (Fig.
1f), but the total number of events and the genes that they occurred in varied among patients, from 45 events in 18 genes down to 1 event in 1 gene (Fig.
1f).
These data also revealed that the precise pattern of cryptic splicing is relatively unique to each patient, although several genes are mis-spliced in up to 15 patients.
For comparison, we analysed RNA-seq data from SLE monocytes (Fig.
1i), interferon-treated healthy donor neutrophils (Fig.
1j), Sjögren’s disease neutrophils (Fig.
1j), and two publicly available RNA-seq datasets of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from patients with SLE (n = 36 total) (Fig.
1k) using our pipeline and found that only one of the cryptic splicing events in monocytes and two in one SLE PBMC dataset, suggesting that these patterns of cryptic splicing are unique to neutrophils in SLE.
Similarly, the acute myeloid cell line AML14, which represents an immature myeloid phenotype, lacked any cryptic splicing observed in SLE neutrophils.
These datasets had higher sequencing depth, providing greater sensitivity for detecting splicing events than our SLE neutrophils (Supplementary Fig.
2a).
Cryptic splicing correlated with interferon-inducible genes (Supplementary Fig.
2b), but not with anti-nuclear autoantibodies (ribonucleoprotein, Sm antigen, double-stranded DNA, Sjögren's-syndrome-related antigen A (SSA)), SLE disease activity index (SLEDAI), or steroid use (Supplementary Fig.
2c).
A subset of cryptic events, particularly in many interferon-inducible genes, correlated with higher expression in those individuals with the cryptic events.
However, in more than half of the genes, there was no such correlation (Supplementary Fig.
3a–d).
This was also observed by calculating the per cent-spliced in (PSI) for the cryptic splicing events: for many cryptic events, PSI showed minimal change, although for the majority of cryptic splicing events PSI was much altered (Supplementary Fig.
3e).

Using RiboSplitter, we translated the observed cryptic splicing events into peptide sequences. The total number of 9-mer and 15-mer cryptic peptides that were optimal for class I and class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) binding, respectively, varied between patients (Fig. 1g). To evaluate whether these peptides could bind MHC and be presented to T cells, we determined MHC class I and II haplotypes for each patient using arcasHLA (Supplementary Table 2) and ranked peptides derived from their individual set of novel amino acid sequences for binding using NetMHCpan-4.1 and NetMHCIIpan-4.026. We only considered peptides that did not match any known human protein sequences in Ensemble and in secondary BLAST searches. Individual patients with SLE varied in the number of potential neoantigen peptides with predicted high-affinity binding to their own haplotype of class I or II molecules (Fig. 1h): 86 peptides from 46 genes ranked in the top 2nd percentile, 65 of them in the top 0.5th percentile.
Validation of cryptic splice variants
To experimentally confirm cryptic mRNA splicing events, we designed PCR primers flanking the splicing event that were designed to yield an amplicon of diagnostic size. In a patient with SLE with the multi-exon skip in USP18, this variant was visualized by the appearance of an amplicon corresponding to the predicted 207 bp (Fig. 2a). Sanger sequencing of this band verified its identity as the joined exons 6 and 11. In addition, there were bands of approximately 300 bp and 450 bp, representing the skip of 3 or 2 exons (rather than 4). articles.full_text:
Abstract
Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2.
Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3.
Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals.
This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression.
We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated ‘pseudobulk’ counts.
We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes.
We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types.
By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations.
Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have revealed hundreds of thousands of association signals between genetic variants and human diseases and traits4, but the modes of action by which most of these variants affect phenotypes remain to be characterized, especially non-coding variants. The characterization of the impact of genetic variants on gene expression—known as expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) mapping—can help linking variants to the putative genes they regulate1,5,6,7,8,9, thus identifying the genes and pathways involved in disease pathogenesis, which is a critical step in identifying opportunities for therapeutic intervention10.
However, important limitations remain. First, eQTL mapping has traditionally been limited to common genetic variation (minor allele frequency (MAF)) greater than 1–5%) due to relatively small sample sizes and the widespread use of genotyping arrays, which do not accurately genotype most rare variants and complex structural variants11, compared with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) approaches. Second, eQTLs are extremely context specific, with many studies demonstrating that genetic variants frequently affect gene expression levels in ways detectable only in specific tissues3, sorted cell types6,10,12,13 or on stimulation14,15. Single-cell eQTL mapping has further demonstrated that the effects of many genetic variants on gene expression can only be detected within specific cell types and even transient cellular states3,16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23.
Here we introduce phase 1 of the TenK10K (up to 10,000 cells for 10,000 individuals) study, encompassing 5.4 million cells from 1,925 individuals of European ancestry selected from a broader cohort of 2,103 individuals. In accompanying papers, we leverage the same dataset to investigate the effect of tandem repeat variation on gene expression24 and the putative causal links between gene expression measurements and human diseases and traits25, and an overlapping set of samples to explore the impact of genetic variation on chromatin accessibility26.
Here we use an association method we recently developed, SAIGE-QTL27, to map common-variant and rare-variant single-cell eQTLs across immune cell types. We identify more than 150,000 common-variant effects and more than 30,000 rare-variant effects on gene expression, including signals for nearly 5,000 genes (roughly 25%) with no previously reported eQTLs in a large blood eQTL study5. We propose a framework for quantifying the extent of cell-type specificity or sharedness of eQTLs and show that about half of the effects are found in only one or a few cell types, and almost none are ubiquitous across all. We perform statistical colocalization between our eQTLs and 60 disease phenotypes and blood traits, identifying more than 60,000 colocalization events for more than 5,000 genes, providing potential molecular mechanisms in almost 900 genes associated with human phenotypic variation. We use a biologically driven deep learning method, scDeepID, to identify continuous cell states related to cell function and map more than 15,000 eQTLs that vary dynamically along those states. Finally, we identify 164 independent genetic variants that regulate the abundance of cell states.

We collected and sequenced PBMCs from all individuals, yielding an average of 2,825 cells per individual after quality control (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 and Methods).
Each cell was assigned to their donor of origin by means of demultiplexing and to an immune cell type using a combined approach of reference-based classification and hierarchical clustering as recommended by the single-cell eQTLGen Consortium28 (Methods). Each cell was assigned to one of 28 different cell types, spanning the key expected immune lineages (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 2).
In addition, we generated WGS data for all 1,925 individuals, which was processed and quality-controlled using established pipelines (Methods). We called 66,658,242 sites across single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and insertions and deletions (indels), of which 53,784,018 (80.6%) were rare (MAF  1%) variant sites within ±100 kilobases (kb) of the gene body on single-cell expression profiles (testing all sufficiently expressed genes; Methods). articles.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1Sensorimotor and amygdala activation, but not canonical prefrontal control circuits, indicate emotion regulation capacity.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions3,4,5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

Emotion regulation is a core determinant of mental and physical health1. It encompasses the strategies that people use, intentionally or automatically, to influence their emotional experience. Among these, cognitive reappraisal—changing the interpretation of a situation to alter its emotional impact—has received particular attention in psychology, psychiatry and the broader public. It is central to cognitive-behavioural therapy and linked to resilience, lower symptom burden and improved daily affect1.
Neuroimaging studies have extensively mapped the neural basis of reappraisal. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) consistently implicates a network of lateral and medial prefrontal regions, often along with reduced amygdala activation during reappraisal of negative stimuli2. These findings have informed neuromodulatory interventions for emotion regulation deficits6,7,8. Still, they are based primarily on within-person designs that contrast experimental conditions such as ‘reappraise’ versus ‘view without regulation’ in the same individuals, and many studies and broader theories extend these neural within-person mechanisms to explain between-person individual differences in well-being or psychopathology4,5. This extension is not necessarily warranted.
Extending within-person neural mechanisms to explain between-person differences risks the ecological fallacy9: associations at one level need not hold at the other. For instance, people who habitually use reappraisal report better well-being than others. However, in daily life, reappraisal often occurs in response to stressors and may therefore coincide with worse-than-average momentary mood.
Compounding this, prefrontal regions that are engaged during reappraisal also participate in working memory, response selection and pain processing10—limiting their specificity as emotion-related markers of regulatory function. Task designs, moreover, may not mirror naturalistic regulation, raising questions about ecological validity and relevance for individual-difference research11,12. A recent systematic review found partial effect convergence in prefrontal and amygdala circuits, but studies were underpowered13 (median n = 25) and too heterogeneous for formal meta-analysis3. In turn, meta-analyses on reappraisal in mental disorders have yielded mixed results, with inconsistent findings in the prefrontal cortex4,14,15.
To resolve this, we conducted a preregistered consortium analysis of 40 fMRI datasets on the neurobiology of emotion regulation capacity (NIDER consortium; n = 2,175; Methods, ‘Consortium procedures’ and Supplementary Table 1)—approximately 20 times larger than previous efforts3—with sufficient power to detect even small between-person associations (r = 0.10; Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’). In this context, reappraisal capacity refers to individual differences in whether, and how effectively, people use reappraisal to reduce negative affect. We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal. Prior work has linked these three indices with each other and with prefrontal activity during reappraisal3,16,17,18,19. To our knowledge, this assumption has not been tested at scale. Notably, the most widely used trait questionnaires are generally understood to index self-reported habitual tendencies to reappraise rather than the ability to implement reappraisal. We nonetheless included them given their proposed functional link to such ability16,17,18 and their widespread use.
We explored whether the three indices converge on a shared core, and whether any of them relate to activity in canonical emotion regulation circuits during common reappraisal tasks2. Our findings have direct implications for neuromodulatory interventions, biomarker development and the validity of individual-difference research in affective neuroscience.
Divergence of capacity indices

If these three indices represent a similar core construct, or are otherwise functionally related, they should show a meaningful association. Individual consortium study teams calculated the correlations between the three indices of reappraisal capacity based on a standardized coding protocol using functionally predefined regions of interest, ensuring that higher values on each index indicate higher reappraisal capacity. Study-level results were aggregated with random-effects meta-analyses, which is statistically equivalent to person-level random-effects mega-analysis for the preregistered analyses and was intended to circumvent data sharing thresholds (Supplementary Methods, ‘Meta- vs mega-analytic approaches’). The evidence for null results was further quantified using Bayes factors (Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’).
There was a statistically significant association between amygdala down-regulation and task-based affective ratings (P = 0.010; Table 1 and Forest plots in Extended Data Figs. 1–3). As hypothesized, participants with stronger down-regulation of the amygdala via cognitive reappraisal showed a better down-regulation of task-based affective ratings. Yet, the effect size was comparatively small (r = 0.08): To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80%, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).
There was no significant association between trait questionnaires and either outcome—that is, amygdala down-regulation or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.06, BF10 ≤ 0.16; Table 1). Confidence intervals ruled out even small effect sizes (r = 0.10), for which statistical power was above 88% given the maximal observed between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.07; Supplementary Fig. 1). The overlap (shared variance) between the three indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity is shown in Fig. 1, which indicates no shared overlap between all three. Bayes factors substantially favoured the null hypothesis for associations with trait questionnaires (BF10 ≤ 0.16). Between-study heterogeneity was not statistically significant in any of the three tests (P > 0.17) and was particularly small for the non-significant correlations (τ = 0.00 and 0.06), indicating that these null findings are unlikely to be explained by differences in study design.
All studies made use of trait questionnaires that primarily assess beliefs about habitual reappraisal use. Although relations to implementation ability, as measured by experiments, are theoretically and empirically expected16,17,18, trait questionnaires that directly measure beliefs about such abilities might show stronger associations. To test this, we performed a subsequent analysis based on three large studies that additionally administered modified versions of the emotion regulation questionnaire to capture such beliefs about abilities20. Supporting the null results for habit questionnaires, there was substantial evidence against an association between these ability trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings (BF10 = 0.13). By contrast, the association between trait ability questionnaires and amygdala down-regulation was statistically significant (P = 0.010), but in the opposite direction, meaning that beliefs in higher reappraisal capacity were related to less effective down-regulation of the amygdala. This represents strong evidence against an effect in the expected direction (one-sided BF10 = 0.05).

Abstract
Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes1,2.
However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk.
Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells.
Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8+ T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8+ T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy.
These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8+ T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade.
In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8+ T cell stemness and resistance to therapy.
Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have substantially improved the prognosis and survival of patients with various solid cancers3, including melanoma4,5,6, non-small cell lung cancer7,8 and bladder cancer9,10,11. However, the overall response rate remains around 30%, which leaves many patients without clinical benefit12. The mechanisms that underlie this heterogeneous response remain poorly understood, which limits the ability to predict and improve ICI efficacy in individual patients.
Recent advances in immunotherapy suggest that the tumour stroma has a pivotal role in shaping responses to ICIs, functioning both as a facilitator and a barrier to effective antitumour immunity1,2. Diverse stromal components engage in continuous reciprocal communication with tumour cells to influence tumour progression and therapeutic responses. A major challenge in defining how the tumour stroma shapes ICI responses is the lack of experimental systems that accurately recapitulate these dynamic, multicellular interactions with high human relevance. Recent advances, including patient-derived xenografts13,14,15, humanized mouse models16,17,18 and ex vivo culture of human tumour tissues using air–liquid interface (ALI) techniques19,20, have improved the representation of human tumour architecture and complexity. However, precise manipulation and tracking of individual cell types and their interactions in these systems are challenging, which limits detailed mechanistic analyses of tumour–stroma–immune crosstalk.
In this study, we developed patient-derived, combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids from individuals with renal cell carcinoma (RCC). These assembloids recapitulate dynamic interactions among tumour cells, CAFs and CD8+ T cells and reflect patient-specific responses to immunotherapy. By integrating genetically manipulated assembloids with humanized mouse models, we identified a signalling axis that governs tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk and the mechanisms that underlie differential responses to ICIs. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into heterogeneous ICI responses and establish a platform for developing strategies to enhance immunotherapeutic efficacy across diverse malignancies.
Generation of patient-specific RCC assembloids
To investigate the cellular and molecular basis of heterogeneous ICI responses in RCC, we established patient-specific tumour assembloids21 that faithfully recapitulate therapeutic responses by reconstituting autologous tumour cells, CAFs and tumour-infiltrating immune (TII) cells from RCC tissue samples (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Pretreatment tumour tissue samples from six patients before ICI therapy were used to generate tumour organoids (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 1). Organoids from all patients were successfully propagated; however, with prolonged culture, cells negative for carbonic anhydrase IX (CA9−) progressively dominated, an effect that is probably due to in vitro growth advantages (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To overcome this technical difficulty, CA9+ and CA9− cells were isolated and separately maintained as distinct organoid populations (Extended Data Fig. 1d). The resulting CA9+ organoids contained canonical clear-cell RCC-associated somatic alterations, including VHL mutations and other recurrent driver events, whereas no detectable VHL mutations were identified in the CA9− organoids (Extended Data Fig. 1e–h and Supplementary Data 2). Both populations maintained clear-cell histology with distinct morphological and immunohistological features (Extended Data Fig. 1d).
Next, we generated patient-specific RCC assembloids by reconstituting CA9+ and CA9− populations with patient-matched CAFs and TII cells at ratios reflecting the cellular composition of the corresponding primary tumours. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Patient-derived CAFs and TII cells were isolated and expanded separately (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3), a process that largely preserved their major cellular compositions relative to the corresponding parental tumours. CAFs exhibited a phenotype similar to myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs) and comparable proportions of cells expressing key markers (Extended Data Fig. 2a–e). Conversely, TII cells preserved the overall composition of major immune cell populations despite modest shifts in specific subpopulations in some patients (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c).
To characterize assembloid formation over time, we performed time-course analyses at days 0, 3, 5 and 7. Cultures were initiated from dissociated single cells at day 0, and no organized tissue architecture was evident up to day 3 (Fig. 1a,b). Multicellular organization emerged by day 5, and by day 7, the assembloids recapitulated key structural and histological features of the matched parental tumours. In detail, tumour cells were associated with CAFs and were infiltrated by immune cells while maintaining >90% cell viability throughout the culture period (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). The assembloids also retained the genetic alterations of the parental tumours (Fig. 1c,d, Extended Data Fig. 4d–i and Supplementary Data 3).
We also performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of RCC assembloids and directly compared them with the corresponding parental tumour datasets at single-cell resolution. Through integrated analysis, we identified the major tumour microenvironment (TME) compartments in both RCC assembloids and parental tumours, including tumour cells, CAFs and diverse immune populations (Fig. 1e,f). Although cell-type proportions varied across patients, assembloids and matched parental tumours showed overall concordance in tumour, stromal and immune cell composition (Fig. 1g,h). Moreover, cell-type-specific transcriptomic comparisons revealed high similarity between assembloids and their matched parental tumours across multiple cell types (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 4j–o).
Notably, all patient-specific RCC assembloids faithfully recapitulated the therapeutic responses of their corresponding patients to ICIs. Treatment of RCC assembloids with anti-PD-1 antibodies for 7 days induced substantial tumour reduction and increased apoptosis in four patient-derived assembloids (P-1, P-4, P-5 and P-6). This result was confirmed through cleaved caspase-3 staining in tumour cells, and by the minimal apoptosis observed in CAFs and immune cells (Fig. 1j–l). By contrast, assembloids from two patients (P-2 and P-3) did not exhibit significant tumour cell death (Fig. 1j–l). The responses of individual assembloids to anti-PD-1 mirrored the clinical outcomes of the corresponding patients from which the assembloids were generated (Fig. 1m). Together, these findings establish that patient-specific RCC assembloids generated from autologous tumour cells, CAFs and immune cells are a robust experimental platform that recapitulates the histopathology and ICI responsiveness of parental tumours in the cohort analysed.

This result was consistent with the patterns observed in matched parental tumour tissue samples (Fig. 2b). Notably, depletion of stem-like CD8+ T cells markedly impaired anti-PD-1 responsiveness and tumour cell killing (Extended Data Fig. 5a), which indicated that these cells are required for effective anti-PD-1 responses23,24,27,28,29,30,31,32.

Abstract
The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors1. Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle2. Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

The oxidation of carbon fuels within the mitochondria is responsible for more than 95% of human ATP production1,3. Dietary carbohydrates supply energy beginning with glycolysis, producing pyruvate that is either reduced to lactate in the cytosol by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), which also regenerates NAD+, or is imported into the mitochondria for oxidation by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle4. Circulating lactate turnover exceeds that of glucose in mammalian physiology5,6, establishing lactate production as the dominant mode of cytosolic NAD+ regeneration. Lactate has the same oxidation state as glucose, is a major circulating oxidative fuel source in both fasted and fed mammalian physiology, and is consumed primarily by the heart, skeletal muscle and kidney7,8,9.
Conventional models posit that lactate oxidation starts with the generation of cytosolic pyruvate by LDH, which is subsequently imported into the mitochondria by the obligate heterodimeric mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC, encoded by Mpc1 and Mpc2)2,10. This arrangement leads to competition between LDH and glycolytic enzymes for NAD+, restricting flux through these pathways when metabolic demand is high (Fig. 1a). However, the heart can oxidize both lactate and glucose simultaneously in response to energetic demand11,12,13, suggesting that there might be distinct routes for pyruvate and lactate oxidation14,15.
Here we reconcile the conflict between lactate, glucose and pyruvate oxidation by demonstrating that MCT1, which is canonically on the plasma membrane, is also present on the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) of cardiomyocytes. MCT1 is necessary for the uptake and oxidation of lactate, providing metabolic redundancy that sustains cardiac energetics. Genetic ablation of MCT1 abolishes mitochondrial lactate oxidation, disrupts adaptation to neurohormonal, hemodynamic or ischemic stress and accelerates the development of heart failure with enhanced mortality.
Glucose oxidation independent of the MPC
To test the prevailing model of lactate oxidation in heart, we utilized our previously described tamoxifen-inducible cardiac-specific Mpc1-knockout mice (Mpc1fl/fl; αMHCMerCreMer+/−, hereafter Mpc1iCKO) to quantify the extent to which the oxidation of glucose and lactate in the myocardium requires the MPC16.
We implanted jugular vein catheters into 4 week post-tamoxifen injection (wpi) Mpc1iCKO mice and Mpc1fl/fl littermate controls with normal cardiac function and subsequently infused awake mice with [U-13C]glucose or [U-13C]lactate to reach stable serum enrichment (Extended Data Fig.
1a).
Hearts and serum were then collected for isotopic labelling analysis of metabolites by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) (Fig.
1b).
Similar to prior reports, we observed a rapid appearance of [1,2,3-13C]lactate in serum upon [U-13C]glucose infusion and labelled glucose with [U-13C]lactate infusion, reflecting high rates of interconversion between these metabolites6 (Extended Data Fig.
1b,c).
There was no difference in total serum isotopic enrichment and endogenous rates of glucose and lactate appearance between Mpc1fl/fl and Mpc1iCKO mice (Extended Data Fig.
1b–e).
We anticipated that the contribution of glucose to TCA cycle metabolites and thus cardiac ATP production would decrease in Mpc1iCKO mice.
Unexpectedly, we observed that the glucose carbon contribution to lactate, pyruvate and TCA cycle metabolites increased in Mpc1iCKO mice compared with controls, a finding also reported by others17,18 (Fig.
1c).
13C labelling in the M+1 and M+2 isotopomers of representative TCA metabolites succinate and malate from Mpc1iCKO hearts was increased, but no changes in M+3 isotopomer labelling were seen, indicating enhanced glucose contribution through acetyl-CoA entry to the TCA cycle19 (Extended Data Fig.
1f,g).
The contribution of lactate carbon to TCA cycle metabolites trended lower in Mpc1iCKO hearts but was not significantly different for any individual metabolite (Fig.

Using a linear algebra-based approach6, our combined glucose and lactate infusion data showed that Mpc1iCKO hearts used the same total amount of carbohydrate-sourced fuel to supply the TCA cycle, but that it was paradoxically shifted towards glucose in MPC1-deficient hearts (Extended Data Fig.
1j).
We performed additional infusions of other major cardiac fuels (palmitate, oleate and 3-hydroxybutyrate) to determine whether Mpc1iCKO mice displayed systemic alterations in cardiac fuel choice that may have confounded our glucose and lactate tracing results (Extended Data Fig.
1k–m).
However, the contributions of these fuels to the cardiac TCA cycle were not statistically different from controls, suggesting that heart glucose metabolism is resilient to loss of the MPC in the short term.

Lactate is a fuel for cardiomyocytes
Our data from young Mpc1iCKO mice suggests the presence of an MPC-independent mitochondrial import pathway for glucose and lactate carbons. To better understand the cardiomyocyte-intrinsic metabolism of glucose and lactate, we used primary cultured adult cardiomyocytes (ACMs). Control ACMs were competent to oxidize glucose as assessed by 13C incorporation into TCA cycle metabolites (Fig. 1e). However, when unlabelled lactate was added to standard lactate-free ACM culture medium (DMEM) containing [U-13C]glucose, labelling from glucose was attenuated, suggesting a strong preference for lactate over glucose oxidation (Fig. 1e). Lactate consumption was not affected by loss of MPC1 as ACMs from Mpc1iCKO and Mpc1fl/fl mice metabolized lactate into TCA metabolites equivalently (Extended Data Fig. 2a).
Mpc1iCKO mice develop heart failure16,17,20,21 and we investigated whether changes in glucose and lactate oxidation were now present. Mpc1iCKO mice at 16–20 wpi exhibited reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and hypertrophy (Fig. 1f,g). To successfully introduce stable isotopes into these mice with heart failure, we adopted our protocol to employ a tail vein catheter infusion administered under anaesthesia. Oxidation of glucose and lactate carbon was significantly reduced in failing Mpc1iCKO hearts, despite similar pyruvate and lactate labelling indicating that carbohydrate uptake was not altered (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Total cardiac glycogen was unchanged (Extended Data Fig. 2g). The observed reduction in the oxidation of infused lactate in failing Mpc1iCKO hearts support the hypothesis that there is an MPC1-independent path for lactate oxidation that supports cardiac function.
To identity a potential alternative mitochondrial transporter of lactate, we conducted immunoblot analysis of purified mitochondria from myocardium and observed expression of the lactate transporter MCT1 (encoded by Slc16a1) in the mitochondrial fraction of healthy and failing Mpc1iCKO hearts (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 2h,i). MCT1 has previously been reported in mitochondria from cardiac tissue22,23. Analysis of published single-nuclei RNA-sequencing data from human hearts showed that SLC16A1 transcripts are predominantly expressed in cardiomyocytes24 (Extended Data Fig. 2j). Notably, MCT1 expression was increased in the mitochondria of young healthy Mpc1iCKO hearts but not failing hearts (Extended Data Fig. 2i,k,l). The existence of mitochondrial lactate import and metabolism has been proposed for decades, but its physiological relevance and mechanistic basis remain actively contested within the field25,26.
MCT1 is required for lactate oxidation
To test whether MCT1 can provide an alternative mechanism for carbohydrate carbon entry and oxidation in mitochondria, we repeated our [U-13C]glucose tracing in young, healthy Mpc1iCKO mice cotreated with AZD3965 (AZD), a potent MCT1 inhibitor with selectivity over MCT227. AZD treatment in control mice had no effect on the oxidation of glucose carbon as measured by TCA cycle metabolite labelling (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). However, when AZD was administered to Mpc1iCKO mice, glucose labelling of TCA cycle substrates was ablated. Although MCT1 may have a role in the transport of lactate across both the plasma membrane and IMM, our tracing data support an essential mitochondrial role, as glucose carbon uptake is not dependent on MCT1 activity. Overall, our data suggest functional redundancy between MCT1 and the MPC for the uptake of three-carbon equivalents into the mitochondria.
